speechtext:
This is the clause which provides for the appointment of one or more deputy commissioners. I do not think there should be any objection to the regularizing by statute of what has been done recently by order in council, as the minister himself pointed out in his remarks on the resolution stage on May 25. However, there is something which appears in clause 1 of the bill which, to my mind, is not quite consistent with what the minister indicated on May 25 would be done in this respect. I refer to his remarks as reported at page 5072 of Hansard where he said as follows:
This position-
Referring to the position of deputy commissioner.
-was established on the first of April, 1932 and since that time, as is obvious to all of us, the responsibilities and the strength of the force have increased greatly. The senior assistant commissioner, under the authority of an order in council dated March 26, 1953, now receives the same rate of pay as that authorized for the deputy commissioner and is performing duties of equal responsibility. We consider that it is desirable to regularize this situation by providing in the establishment for two deputy commissioners and by cancelling the establishment and salary provision of the senior assistant commissioner. There are, therefore, as is obvious, no financial implications involved.

Under clause 1 of this bill they are establishing the position of one or more deputy commissioners but we are still left with one or more assistant commissioners. It seems to me that it would be obvious that one of those assistant commissioners, if more than one, would be senior assistant commissioner. It is not quite the same as what the minister indicated in his remarks or at least according to the impression that I drew from the minister's remarks on May 25. Yes, I will be glad to do so, and I think I should do so because I wish to correct an inaccuracy in my previous explanation at the resolution stage. As I correctly pointed out then the purpose of the bill is to put all members of the force who, having served with the force for ten years or upwards, have been discharged for misconduct or inefficiency, in the same position of entitlement to a reduced pension whether they are retired under parts II and III of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act on the one hand or are retired under part V of the act on the other.
In explaining this purpose I inadvertently transposed the numbers of these parts and as a result said that the part V pension scheme did not provide for such a pension in the event of a member being discharged for inefficiency or misconduct and that the pension schemes under parts II and III did provide


for such a pension to members so discharged. The facts are the reverse, namely that part V now makes provision for this type of reduced pension for those who have served for ten years and are retired for misconduct or inefficiency whereas parts II and III do not provide for such reduced pension where the member has been discharged for these reasons.
The purpose of the bill therefore is to amend parts II and III to provide such reduced pension and thus equalize in this respect the position of Royal Canadian Mounted Police pensioners under parts II and III with the position of pensioners under part V. This purpose is accomplished by clause 3 of the bill.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Martin for the second reading of Bill No. 422, to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Is the minister not going to explain the bill?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
This bill mainly seeks to do three things. It seeks to redefine the
present offence of trafficking and also endeavours to create a new offence of trafficking based on the illegal possession of drugs. It also provides for extending the powers of the governor in council to make certain regulations for the more effective enforcement of the measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think every person in the house is in agreement that this bill is necessary, because the regulations cannot be made too strong with respect to people who traffic in drugs. To destroy a person physically and mentally by the use of drugs is a crime that should carry a very heavy penalty. So far as the bill is concerned, the rights of those who are entitled to use narcotic drugs, veterinarians, doctors and druggists, seem to be protected.

The question then remains to put in legal terms what can be done to stop the horrible traffic in drugs.
I do not believe that the traffic in drugs in Canada has reached the height that it has in some countries, but we are a young and growing nation and as our population increases there is no doubt that we will be faced with greater difficulty in this regard. In central Canada the situation possibly is not as bad as in areas such as Vancouver and Victoria with seaports facing the Orient. The difficulty would seem to be greater there, and at those places there is the greatest possible chance of such drugs being illegally brought into the country. I am in complete agreement that the penalties should be made very severe. Possibly it can be argued that making penalties severe may bring about more evasion, but in my opinion the penalties cannot be too severe.
We make regulations in the Criminal Code with regard to manslaughter, murder and crimes of that type. Here we are dealing with something that causes the total destruction of people mentally and physically. Worst of all, we are led to believe that the people who illegally traffic in drugs try to induce young people to become addicts. Having that in mind, we should go over very carefully the clauses of the bill having to do with penalties. I am absolutely in favour of making the penalties as severe as possible in order that this traffic may be curbed. Possibly one of the worst of all the drugs in which these people traffic is heroin, and it is very easy for a person to become addicted to heroin. Therefore every possible channel should be explored of curbing this trade. I am in full agreement with the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to say a word in support of the bill. I was very glad to hear the remarks that have just been made by a medical man who is in close contact with the problem in a professional way. It seems to me he is quite right in stating that the penalties for trafficking in drugs cannot be too severe. Traffickers must be penalized to the greatest possible extent, but I think that something more must be done than merely to punish them. In years past we have had the league of nations trying to deal with this problem internationally. We have the United Nations commission on narcotic drugs, and various agreements and protocols have been signed for the purpose of limiting the production and export of narcotic drugs. I believe that a protocol on the production of opium was agreed upon last June by the 83276-336
1,	1954	5305
Opium and Narcotic Drug Act United Nations Organization and that it is to come into effect when some twenty-five nations have signed. I was going to ask the minister if Canada is one of the signatories to this protocol? She was not at the time the report of the Department of External Affairs was published.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: She will be.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But she is not yet?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
However, I am very glad to know we are signing that protocol. In 1946 I had the opportunity of representing Canada on the committee of the economic and social council which dealt with narcotics. I have a very vivid recollection of the discussion that occurred there, and the terrible effects of this drug on those who become addicted to it. I believe that is fairly well known. I agree with the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) when he says one of the real dangers is that young people may become addicted to this very destructive habit, and that this is encouraged by people who are criminals and who should be treated as criminals.
What I really wanted to say was that I do not think this is enough. While we should imprison and penalize the trafficker to the fullest extent possible, what we need is some institution, not a prison, in which those who have become addicted can be treated. I do not think placing an addict in jail is the proper manner in which to treat him. What we need is a proper institution in which those people who have become addicted can be placed and can be looked after until they are weaned of the habit, whether that takes six months, a year or five years. This is a problem with which every country in the world is faced. We are no exception to it. I believe we have a very fine organization endeavouring to locate these traffickers in drugs.
It is so easy to bring these drugs into the country. I mean to conceal them, I do not mean it is easy in the sense in which that term might apply, but the quantities are so small there are various ways of bringing them into the country. I feel we should congratulate the narcotics enforcement branch on the excellent work that is done in this regard. What I feel is needed is not only a bill of this description, with the right of the governor general in council to make regulations that will help stamp out this traffic; we should try to do something further in the way of rehabilitation of the people who have become victimized. I do not think this bill perhaps does all that is required to be done, but I think the house should give

Opium and Narcotic Drug Act its warm support and approval to the increase in the penalty for trafficking in drugs, and so we support the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to indicate our support for the measure that is now before us. While I am doing so, I should like to underline what was said by the leader of the C.C.F. party as to the need for some institution where addicts in this country can receive the kind of treatment they require. I do not look upon those unfortunate individuals who have become addicts as criminals at all. They are driven by extreme necessity when they form the habit; that is, people will do anything to get the required doses of the drug in order to satisfy their craving. They are driven by that necessity to procure the necessary drugs. They are driven to go amongst young people who may be completely innocent of the designs upon them.
There must be some place where these people can get what they require for the time being, no matter how long it may be, until such time as they are either weaned of the habit or become so confirmed in the habitual use of the drugs that they have to be confined. Something will have to be done along that line, otherwise we cannot hope to protect our young people. I am told that in some of the high schools in our country certain young people have been circulating amongst the students urging them to try the drugs for the first time. For each new one that they secure, the criminal who is behind the whole business will give the student the satisfaction of a cut dose of the drug itself; that sort of thing is going on in some of the schools in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: This is too important a subject to exaggerate. The teen-age problem has been greatly exaggerated, and I am sure my hon. friend would not want to give the impression that it is greater than it is.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
No, not for one second. As a matter of fact, it is bad enough if it only happens to two or three. It is so easy to make these students complete slaves to the use of the drugs that if there are only one or two that is bad enough. It is just as bad as murder, and in some respects it is worse. It is for that reason I am pleased to see a stiffening of the penalties attached to those who would extend the drug traffic.
I merely wanted to say that there is the necessity for some place, I do not know what you would call it, an institution of some kind where habitual users could get whatever supplies they required without having to go out and procure or earn the supplies. Whether or not that could be done, or

whether it is practical, I do not know. Certainly everything that could be done by the government to put a stop to the extension of the traffic ought to be done, and we will support them because it is a good thing. We like the bill as it now stands, since it imposes heavier penalties and we want to give the maximum backing to the enforcement officers in every way possible to control this drug traffic.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
This is a problem that has been given very intensive study in my own city by a very competent committee under the chairmanship of Dr. Wallace Wilson. As you know, Dr. Wilson is the western medical supervisor for the Department of Veterans Affairs, and an outstanding man in his field. Gathered with him on that committee he had prosecuting attorneys, attorneys who specialized in defence, and men of outstanding calibre from the university who specialized in drugs, as well as a number of experienced business and professional men. This committee made a thorough study of this problem of drugs and drug addiction.
Unfortunately the last report issued by the committee is now some two years old. However, the poignant points of that committee report still stand. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister-no doubt he is aware of it-and to the attention of the house that, without exception, this crime of trafficking in drugs is the most heinous of which we could possibly conceive in our modern civilization.
I could not agree more than I do with the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) when they say that this is a problem of great magnitude and one that, in essence, requires considerable watching at all times, and additional increases in penalties for offenders.
There are some sections of the report to which I have referred that I do not think we could adopt in this country at the present time; but there are points in it that should be read. For instance, we all know that where you find perversions of various kinds, somewhere along the line drugs enter into the picture. Additionally, invariably the first offenders, who might be termed exhibitionists, and who have no criminal desires to murder or to destroy, eventually, with the continued use of drugs, with all their nefarious effects, not only become exhibitionists but also become more intense in their addiction to drugs. Consequently, as a result thereof, they are a greater menace and danger to the society we represent in Canada.

There have appeared in the press some objections to statements made respecting the degree of criminality existing in Vancouver. Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much interest to all that has been said by the previous speakers. I certainly agree with them that this bill brings to the attention of the house a very serious problem in Canada and one which is most serious in the coastal areas. I am certain that all hon. members will be in agreement in their support of the intent behind the bill, especially as it deals with the increasing of penalties imposed against those who traffic illegally in drugs in this country.
The bill is comprehensive in that it covers the sections of the statute that deal with trafficking, licensing and possession. Therefore the amendments before us open up the possibility of a comprehensive study of the narcotics situation, and the kind of law we should have not only to deal with the traffic in drugs, but also with those who are in possession of them. I want to add my words to those of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that perhaps under the amending sections there should be more accent on the curative instead of the punitive.

Opium and Narcotic Drug Act
As was pointed out by the previous speaker, there is undoubtedly a very serious situation on the Pacific coast. The hon. member said there were 14,000 known addicts in Canada, and he was corrected by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) who, I believe, said there were approximately
3,000.	However, Mr. Speaker, I was going to use the figure of 5,000, on the basis that that was the report which Canada made to the United Nations committee which is studying this matter.
This matter of narcotics very forcibly came to my attention about 15 years ago in the city of Vancouver when a friend of mine became a drug addict. As he progressed it cost more and more for his needs and he resorted to robbery, and he landed in jail. He landed back in jail upon more than one occasion because he was not cured. He got married, and unfortunately his wife also became an addict. Today, his wife is in a mental institution, as she has been for several years past, and she will never come out. I know from my own personal knowledge of the man that he resorted to robbery only because of his illness and he did not have the money to supply his needs. It can be easily recognized-when it is understood that when you have an addict who actually requires, because of his illness, several capsules a day and he has none, and on the illegal market in Vancouver it costs around $5.50 and $6 a capsule-why he resorts to robbery. That was this man's history for a while. He is no longer in jail. I think I can safely say that he has been a good, respectable and responsible member of society in Canada for a number of years. He still requires a minimum dosage of a narcotic, and he gets it. But because he does get it, as I said, he is a good member of society.
That experience, which started some 15 years ago, interested me in this subject, and over a number of years now I have interviewed a great many drug addicts in and out of jail, I have interviewed authorities, policemen and doctors on this matter. As a result, a special study was made in Vancouver by the member of the legislature for Burnaby, my father, and upon two occasions he got in contact with every doctor in the province of British Columbia on this matter. The reply in the main stated that we would never remove this curse of drug addiction and the problems it gives rise to unless it was handled in a different way. A great many doctors express the view that the law of Canada should be changed to allow them to treat addicts as sick persons, and under medical supervision to supply their medical requirements at cost.

That is correct, Mr. Speaker, but it is not generally known to the people of Canada; nor has there ever been, to my knowledge, an educational program to try to get the addict to go to a doctor and to take the care that a doctor can give, and to receive the minimum narcotic requirements. This study has been made, I know, in a great many countries of the world. It is rather remarkable to note the incidence of drug addiction in a great many other countries of the world compared with our own Dominion of Canada. I have noted especially from the reports that are issued annually by the economic and social council, as a commission on narcotic drugs under the authority of United Nations, that in the countries where there have been educational campaigns and where drug addicts do go to doctors and they get their prescriptions filled at cost, the countries know of their drug addiction and they know who the people are. They keep track of them and because-and this is important-of the registration of drug addicts and their care and treatment at cost price, it has taken the profit out of the illegal trade. When you take the profit out of the illegal trade you strike a body blow at the illicit traffic, because the peddlers are not interested in selling the dope unless they can make a profit, and they are certainly not interested in getting new addicts if they cannot get a profit out of them. I am certain from my study that where there is a concentrated program, as there is in a great many countries of the world, you not only reduce the number of addicts but you almost wipe out the illegal trade itself.
The illegal trade is of very serious proportions in Canada. The most recent figure that I saw was a statement by an R.C.M.P. officer in Vancouver who estimated that somewhere between $5 million and $7 million worth of illegal narcotics are entering Canada through the port of Vancouver. In my estimation, that should make all of us here with responsibility for policy and law give perhaps more consideration than we have in the past to

this problem. When I say that we should give more consideration, I am basing that opinion on the 1952 report of the economic and social council. In that section dealing with Canada -and I presume the report is sent in by Canada-we find on page 14:
It was estimated that there were approximately 5,000 addicts of whom roughly 70 per cent are males. Furthermore, it was reasonable to assume that addiction may be slightly on the increase, in view of the large supplies of heroin entering the country illicitly as evidenced by seizures of this drug and the steady prices maintained in the illicit traffic.
This is important. It goes on:
No definite program of treatment has been formulated.
I think we are negligent, Mr. Speaker- I say "we"-in our responsibility when in the 1952 report we find the statement by Canada that no definite program of treatment has been formulated, while at the same time we admit there are 5,000 addicts in Canada, and that the number is slightly on the increase. The hon. member who spoke just before me mentioned a committee which met in Vancouver over a period of years. I want to make reference to another committee in Vancouver composed of doctors which met under the auspices of the community chest. Under the chairmanship of Dr. Foulks they have been making a study over a period of three years of methods of curing drug addicts, and the other day when it was announced that the Senate had under consideration the appointment of a committee to study the narcotic problem Dr. Foulks, on behalf of this committee, made a statement, and I would like to quote a short paragraph from the press report of his statement. He said:
We have never agreed entirely with the law's approach to drug addiction. Medical men agree that changes are needed in the Drug Act to allow for treatment on a medical basis instead of on a punitive basis.
Now, that is the view of that special committee in Vancouver and, sir, it is in line, I think I can say, with the authoritative views of those who have made a study of this problem on the North American continent.
I would now like to quote, but not extensively, from a man in the United States who is recognized as an outstanding authority. He is Alfred R. Lindesmith, associate professor of sociology, Indiana University. In his book "Opiate Addiction", which I am told is considered almost as a bible on this subject, he has this to say:
The most important basic change which is needed in this country is legislation or the interpretation
Opium and Narcotic Drug Act
of existing legislation so that the prescription of drugs to an addict by a physician is defined as being within the field of medicine.
This would mean that a physician could legally prescribe drugs to an addict and it would give addicts a legitimate low-cost source of supply. This is the way in which English drug laws are interpreted.
At first glance it might seem that such a plan would make opiates more available than they are now and lead to a spread of the habit. However, consideration reveals that the opposite would be the case. In England, where, as has been indicated, doctors do prescribe for addicts, there is much less addiction than in the United States and there is scarcely any smuggling problem.
At present the new addict in this country usually obtains his drugs from illicit sources. Under the proposed plan he would have to obtain his supplies from a doctor registered under the act. Certainly one would expect medical men to exert more of a restraining influence on the spread of addiction than the underworld peddler does. The reduction or the elimination of illegal dealings in opiates would unquestionably remove the greatest source to new addicts now in existence.
The first step in any plan to alleviate this dreadful affliction should be the establishment of control and dispensation at cost of habit forming drugs. With the profit motive gone no effort would be made to encourage its use by private dispensers of narcotics and the drug peddler would of necessity disappear. New addicts would be speedily discovered and through early treatment some of these unfortunate victims might be saved from becoming hopelessly incurable.

I think, sir, that is sufficient to at least bring up the point I have in mind to the effect that there is a difference in the way in which this problem is being approached in other countries compared with Canada. Perhaps we can learn from them and I am certain that the matter is so serious that we have to try and find a new approach. I am speaking personally from my own studies and knowledge of the subject and from the very great help given to me in this by one on whom I rely for his study on this matter, and that is my father, an M.L.A. of British Columbia, who has made a very great study of it. However, I think I am safe in saying, at least as far as British Columbia is concerned, that the majority of physicians, of authorities and


of the people have reached a point where they are prepared to accept a change in outlook and to say: let us be as hard as we can on the peddler but let us tackle the addict himself or herself as a medical problem; let us find ways and means of trying to get them registered, to get them treated and, where no cure is possible, to enable them to receive their requirements in a minimum dosage at a minimum price. I am convinced that if we could get that idea over-I know there are obstacles but I am sure they can be worked out-we would not have, as was shown in the last report on prisoners, 60 drug stores broken into in a twelve-month period. In the majority of cases, when they go after a drug store, they are after narcotics. If we tackle this matter seriously and do something like what I have mentioned I feel strongly that without a doubt it would go a long way toward taking the profit out of the illicit traffic and in that way would go a long way toward wiping out the illegal entry of dope into Canada.
I realize what the problem is, Mr. Speaker. If my memory serves me correctly, in the United States there were either two or three states which endeavoured to give a try-out to establishing centres where an addict could get his requirements. The experiment failed. I know that at least one state has closed up the experiment. However, there is a good reason for that result, namely that addicts from all the surrounding states poured in, thus creating a terrific problem. That is something that should have been expected, Mir. Speaker, because there are no customs or immigration lines between the various states of the United States; and naturally a person who required the narcotic and who did not have the money with which to buy it on the illegal market went into the state where, by registering as an addict, he could get his requirements.
I would be the last one to suggest that anything in the way of a new approach be made in only one province in Canada because that attempt would be just as much doomed to failure as it was in the United States. Action will have to be taken on a national basis, with the procedure the same all across the Dominion of Canada. I know it might be said that we shall have addicts coming up from the United States. That might perhaps be so to some extent, Mr. Speaker, but not to a major extent, in my opinion. Although we have no immigration or customs barriers between our provinces, we do have an international boundary between our country and the United States. Hence it would be far more difficult for any invasion into Canada of drug addicts from the United States. Be

that as it may, the problem is a most serious one. I think we must tackle it with renewed vigour and understanding, and recognize that it should be treated as a medical problem and not one involving punitive measures. Therefore, although I most certainly support ;he endeavours of the government to strengthen the existing act and to make it tougher on the peddlers, I sincerely hope that the minister can see his way clear in the near future really to tackle this problem on a scientific and intelligent basis.

I would urge that the death penalty or life imprisonment be imposed upon anyone caught peddling drugs to minors.

speechtext:
I thank the hon.
member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) for his words of tribute to the law officers who are responsible for the enforcement of this very important measure.
First of all, I should like to take this opportunity of announcing that Canada will, as of January 1 next year, prohibit the legal importation of heroin into this country. This decision is in accordance with the terms of the resolution unanimously adopted by the world health organization in May, 1953, which provided that the manufacture and use of heroin for any purpose be abolished. Canada, of course, supported this resolution which was unanimously approved at the meeting of the narcotics commission of the United Nations a month ago. The implementation of this resolution will not work any

Opium and Narcotic Drug Act hardship or inconvenience on medical practitioners, since other less dangerous drugs with equally effective properties are available in substitution for heroin.
The prohibition of the importation of heroin will not, of course, affect the legitimate use of such stocks of heroin as are at present in this country. It will mean, however, that no further importations of this drug will be permitted, and as heroin is not manufactured in Canada there will be no further supplies available once the stock as of January 1 is exhausted by legitimate agents. While no immediate effect on the incidence of addiction can be expected from the prohibition on the importation of heroin, an eventual reduction in world supplies of this drug will undoubtedly substantially help in reaching a solution of this portion of the problem.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What is the chief source, the legitimate source, of this drug?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
There are several legitimate sources. I do not think it is desirable that I should name the areas at this time. As the hon. member for Winnipeg South said, in at least one instance the drug is supplied with the knowledge of the government of that nation.
It is impossible to say exactly how many persons in Canada are addicted to the use of narcotic drugs. The number is not likely much more than 3,000. The geographical distribution is confined mainly to the larger cities, with the majority being located in Vancouver and the substantial remainder in the cities of Toronto, Montreal, Hamilton, Windsor, Winnipeg, Edmonton and Calgary. In the discussion that we have had thus far, I think the house has indicated that there is a keen interest and a strong desire to cope as effectively as possible with this unfortunate human problem. I cannot agree that there is any country much worse than another. I think that the enforcement agencies on the continent of North America are more effective, however-and are recognized as such-than in any other countries of the world. As the United Nations itself has indicated, the statistics of some countries do not really represent the situation in those countries, whose reporting quite obviously is inadequate. To suggest, as is said officially, that there are only 300 addicts in one country when I happen to know, on the admission of the minister responsible, that there are many thousands, is not to give any indication of what the real situation is.
And so this is a human problem, and the solution is by no means an easy one. It is one for which mankind has been striving


for a long time. I might say to the house that there has been no other problem in my department that has given me more concern, and about which I have spent as much personal time, as this one. It is a very difficult problem and, so far as I am concerned, it is my desire to make as great a contribution to its solution as I can.
Valuable as it has been, the discussion this morning has revealed that there is a great deal of confusion and misunderstanding with respect to the kind of people who are addicted, their motivations, and what we can do to help them. Nothing was said this morning about the decision taken by the government a year ago, which I announced in the house, in our efforts to try to do something not only on the punitive but on the curative side. It will be recognized that under our constitution the punitive aspect is clearly the responsibility of the federal government. Constitutionally, the curative is the responsibility of the provincial governments who, alone, have the primary responsibility for health policy.
Recognizing however that the problem is national, I announced a plan of action a year ago in the house in an effort to try, in cooperation with the provinces, to cope with this matter. As a result we now have operating in British Columbia a committee headed by one of the most distinguished mental health authorities in the country, Dr. George Stevenson, formerly head of the London mental hospital, who is engaged in a most vigorous study of this problem in British Columbia at the present time.
The decision to set up such a committee was arrived at as the result of agreement with the government of British Columbia. The full cost of the committee's operations is being borne by the federal government. The aim is to see whether, from a careful study of the individuals in that province and elsewhere who use drugs, and from a consideration of other situations connected with this problem, we can learn what has not been learned in other jurisdictions in other parts of the world. And just as quickly as that group has made its findings, and they have been submitted, I have told all the provincial governments in Canada that we will be prepared, under the national health program, to consider proposals-which, basically and constitutionally, mind you, are provincial- in an effort to deal with this problem on the curative side.
What the results will be, I do not know, but I do know that the committee will be interested in doing what I, myself, did a year and a half ago when, in company with officers of my department, I visited two

institutions in the United States where an effort is being made to deal with this problem on a curative basis. I told the house about this a year ago. However, this morning's discussion revealed that apparently on that occasion I did not stress sufficiently what I had said.
The effort made in those two institutions was to get drug addicts under their control- control of the doctor, control of the psychiatrist, control of the social psychiatric worker, and the like-to see what could be done. I think I should say that the results have not been very satisfying in those two institutions-the only institutions of their kind in the world.
However, the achievements or the results of this kind of control and treatment are being considered carefully for study here at home. We are also studying the experience of clinics established in a certain number of states in the United States. I am thinking particularly of clinics in Los Angeles where a drug addict could go and, under the supervision of a doctor, receive treatment in given quantity. I can say that those who have given this matter study are wholly convinced that that certainly is no solution. To give unlimited quantities of drugs to addicts is not to help them, and certainly it is not going to result in any successful mitigation of or reduction in the incidence of crime or the amount of addiction. Those clinics were closed because the bitter experience was that they increased the drug addiction habit.
And so, while it may look easy to suggest that one way to control this problem is to give an addict all he needs, until he is satisfied, in the absence of a place where he can be controlled and continuously supervised that solution is one Which does not commend itself to us at this time.
In the two institutions to which I referred there is an abridged form of the unlimited-use procedure. But there the results, likewise, have not been, as I indicated a moment ago, as successful as we had hoped they might be. And so we are faced with this very human problem, this very difficult human problem, that has taken hold of other countries as well as our own.
We are fortunate that our situation is by no means among the worst. I think it is sufficient here to reiterate what I said before, that in spite of the publicity that from time to time has been given to an occasional-I will not say "indiscretion" because the word is not strong enough-to an occasional action on the part of some minors in our country, they do not represent the youth of this land.
In Vancouver, the city where the number of addicts is greatest, in the last two and a

Someone will suggest that the role of the police officer is one which does not suggest a cure or a remedy for this problem. I quite agree that, on the curative or medicinal side, there can be no doubt about that. But we must not let our interest in humanity run away with the practical situation that attends us, because the greater number-and I say this advisedly-the greater number of drug addicts in this country are individuals who, before they began using drugs, were certainly individuals who came within the reach of the law officers of the crown. And the amount of trafficking that goes on among so-called innocent drug addicts is, I am sure, much greater than the house would think was the case. Therefore we have to try and appreciate what we are seeking to do in the bill now before us. We have to try by effective enforcement measures, which are not at the present time what we would like, to deal with certain situations that we want to get at, which I think with these amendments we will be able to get at in the course of the next few months.
This does not represent all that we are going to try to do. I hope that once the Stevenson survey has been completed in Vancouver and other studies in the country have been made pursuant to the activities we shall be able once again, in co-operation with the provinces, to see whether there is not something more that we can do on the curative side. I assure the house of my very deep interest in seeing that this is done. I should say also, contrary to common belief, it is not an easy thing to buy drugs in the illicit market in Canada, and the source of entry is not the city of Vancouver.
Vigorous enforcement has taught drug traffickers to be wary in their transactions. They deal only with persons known to them, and whose bona fides have been established. Hon. members will have read in the press that the police investigators who have lived with and as addicts in order to be accepted by the fraternity in their efforts to expose the traffickers have had a remarkable

I thank the house for its interest in this problem. I am sure that this general debate has been helpful. Regardless of where we sit in this house, we are all engaged in trying to arrest this problem. The amendments to the act which we are dealing with at the moment are relatively simple, but they will give us power more effectively to deal with the very serious problem of trafficking. I hope that survey and that kind of co-operation will give us an opportunity of taking a forward step in this very vital matter.

Mr. Chairman, I find myself in complete agreement with what the minister has said about this. There has been a tendency to regard this as a problem that has been written up in the Sunday supplements and in some of the cheaper literature in a way that appeals to the morbid in our makeup. But I also find myself in agreement with my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South, regarding the question of treatment, and the ability of doctors, druggists and so forth to obtain drugs. Under this first clause I want to say a few words on this matter.
Several times in the debate the minister had to pause to mention the fact that quantities of the drugs could be prescribed by doctors and were available for so-called treatment. In this I wish to pay tribute to the narcotics branch. They have done a wonderful job; but where an addict is registered with the department-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong in this-it is possible to obtain a sufficient amount of the drug to carry him on. Some of these unfortunate people-and they are not all the type we are talking about- become addicts owing to some chronic disease, or something of that nature. This clause will appeal particularly to them.
There is a matter of argument about treatment. Personally, I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South that, in so far as treatment is concerned, it is difficult to believe these people at any time. They are moral degenerates. Again I agree that unless these people are under supervision there is no chance of treating them as


ambulatory cases, so that the argument regarding total withdrawal versus this kind of treatment is a particularly difficult one. I do feel that they should be placed in an institution. To those people who are arguing against this sort of thing and the whole withdrawal of the drug, and who would like to obtain quantities of it outside, I say it is not a successful type of treatment.
I mention these facts on this first clause in order to correct some of the impressions that have been made. I also agree with the minister that this matter is not so severe in Canada. It is not such a large question, but it is a dangerous one. It is not as great as we would be led to believe by literature of the type I have mentioned. I do not believe that the young people are concerned in this matter. I also agree that those people were probably psychiatric problems before they ever became addicts of the drug. I am glad that the penalties for trafficking are so strong.
It is quite true that those people who sell drugs are making other addicts buy and pay a tremendous price for their drugs, which leads them to some other form of criminal act in order to obtain money with which to buy the drugs. But I simply want to clear up the matter with respect to this form of ambulatory treatment. The drug addict will once in a while write an article for some periodical in which he will complain bitterly that it would be far better for him if he were given a limited supply of this drug. Remember this: none of these people can be trusted. There is only one way in which to treat these people, and that is to put them in an institution, and the question of withdrawal or the cutting down of their drugs can then be considered. To treat them as ambulatory cases is just simply out of the question.
We do get the impression that this is a tremendous problem, and that the young people are faced with it. I was glad to hear the minister decry that sort of thing. I do not think it is so severe as all that, but it does exist. It can become a problem here. Any measure taken to cut down on the trafficking in the supplies of this drug is a measure well taken.
So far as heroin is concerned, there are uses for it, but we can get along very nicely without it. It is one of the most dangerous of drugs, a derivative of opium. Practically all of them come from the one source.
I am glad that every person has spoken in favour of this bill; every person is of the one mind, namely, that this is a dangerous thing; but let us get away from this Sunday supplement lurid thinking, as I suggested, and tackle this question on a common-sense basis,

recognizing that in some areas it does create a problem, particularly where there are traffickers who control some of these people who are led to make money out of it. Let us look at it on that basis. I do not like any suggestion that the youth of Canada has been concerned in this matter at all. I do not believe that. Our country is small; but, as our population grows, the traffic again becomes a problem.
I said I recognized there were uses for heroin, but there are other drugs that can be used in its place. We can get along very well without it. It is the most dangerous of all the drugs that we might consider under this act. The best thing we can do is to consider this act on the same basis and try to deal with the question as the act proposes to deal with the traffickers, those who are concerned in spreading opium derivatives throughout the country and inducing other people to use them. There is a tendency on behalf of the addicts to teach others. They do like to teach other people to become addicts. The whole question so far as this bill is concerned is this. Is the legislation adequate; does it provide suitable penalties; and is there anything further we can do to cut down this traffic in illicit drugs?

Mr. Chairman, on this clause, tying in with clause 1, I should like to say first of all that I appreciate greatly the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare at the conclusion of the debate on second reading of the bill. But on the discussion of clause 1, which now ties in with clause 2, I should like to say that the experience of the hon. member for Lanark, in my opinion, does not tie in first of all with my own personal experience, not as a medical man, but in interviewing a number of addicts in the past fifteen years in British Columbia. It also does not tie in with the findings of doctors in the United States who have made an investigation of a number of cases.

Opium and Narcotic Drug Act
From the remarks of the hon. member for Lanark I gathered that a great majority of those who become drug addicts start from a position of being abnormal. Unfortunately there are not any studies that have been made in Canada on that phase as yet. I greatly appreciate the studies which are now being instituted by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The only record to which I can go back is the record of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. I cannot agree that, in the main, those who start on drug addiction are abnormal. If that statement is correct, according to the studies made in Great Britain it is a reflection on the professions and especially on the doctors' profession. I do not believe that the majority of the doctors' profession who unfortunately become addicts were abnormal when they started on the addiction.	*
I am going to quote from the report of the economic and social council of the commission on narcotic drugs issued by the United Nations and I am going to quote from the report on Great Britain and Northern Ireland. In the report that was made in 1951 by the United Nations, at that time there were reported to be 301 who were addicts receiving medical aid, of whom 75 were doctors, 1 was a dentist and I a pharmacist. I think the fact that that record exists is first of all because of professional pressure and, in the second place, because of the proximity of drugs.
In studying the report of the United Nations I find that in a majority of cases where there is a registration system, it is the professional services which are involved. I do not think they are abnormal when they start. I have had drawn to my attention only three studies of addicts made on the North American continent, and they were made in the United States. Unfortunately I have not the report of the three studies but I have with me a report made on two of the studies. Those studies were made by Dr. Lawrence Kolb of the United States public health service and Dr. Charles Schultz. May I say, sir, that they were investigating only whether persons, as they became drug addicts, were normal or abnormal. I am not going to take up the time of the committee by giving all the results. I shall give only their final conclusion, which was as follows: They admit that normal individuals not only become addicted but that once they are addicted they may have as much difficulty in quitting as does anyone else. Under their evidence it is shown that although the majority, in their estimation, are abnormal at the time they take to drugs, a high percentage are strictly normal at the time they start.


In view of the evidence in Great Britain that the highest percentage of those who take to drugs are from the professional services and from the doctors' services, I think we can take it as conclusive evidence that a great majority start as normal individuals but, because of circumstances, pressures and strains, use drugs as an escape.
I was most interested in one phase of the remarks made by the hon. member for Lanark. That ties in with the most interesting information given us by the Minister of National Health and Welfare with respect to the rights of the medical profession to take care of drug addicts under the present legislation. This is going to be my final statement on this phase of the matter. It may not sit very well with those members of the house who are of the medical profession, but I do want to make this statement because of my interest in the subject, my own experiences in British Columbia over many years and my conversations with a great many doctors in that province and some in other provinces.
I should like to tell the Minister of National Health and Welfare that there are a great many medical men in the dominion who do not realize that they have the right to treat an addict and, if necessary, issue prescriptions to him based on their diagnosis of the case. I know that for a fact because I have talked to a great many doctors. I should like to recommend to the minister that either his own department or the national association of doctors should see to it that the position of doctors under the law is made clear to all practising physicians in Canada. My personal experience is that a great many in the profession are not aware of their legal position.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer. Contrary to the experience of the hon. member for Lanark, and I know he speaks from his own experience, as a layman who has discussed the problem with addicts in western Canada I have found that there are many who want to be cured. There are many who do not want to resort to criminal activities, thereby landing themselves back in jail. On more than one occasion I have tried to refer such men and women who have come to me to the medical profession and I have come up against a very serious obstacle, the reason for which I can quite understand. Under the law as it now exists doctors can take drug addicts as patients and can issue prescriptions for their requirements day by day or week by week. But I want to emphasize that because of their understanding of the law a great many medical men who are humanitarian in outlook and by nature and who would like to look after drug addicts are afraid to do so.

The reason that has been given to me bymore than one British Columbia doctor is that if they started to issue prescriptions to drug addicts, even after their own diagnosis, the first thing that would happen if they issued more than a very few would be that the R.C.M.P. would come right to their offices-I agree with their doing that-and wanting to know why they were issuing that number of prescriptions and why these people required the amount of narcotics they were buying. Perhaps because of ignorance of the situation these doctors said that they might be subjected to investigation and inquiry on account of the narcotic prescriptions they had issued from the point of view of whether they were legal or illegal and whether they were issuing bona fide prescriptions or were actually, in a legal sense, peddling narcotics.
That is a serious situation to me, and I have been told that by more than one doctor in the province of British Columbia who believes that something should be done about addicts. I can understand their worry and their indecision. That is my experience as the result of my conversations with a number of doctors. I want to draw that to the attention of the minister to emphasize what I said on second reading, namely, that I believe that a more intelligent program of spreading knowledge among the profession, the general public and addicts will prove very beneficial to all concerned.

Possibly I was responsible for the use of the word "abnormal", but I was simply pointing out that people who are chronic invalids and are suffering from some chronic condition are led into the position where they do require further supplies because they find it very difficult to cut out the drug entirely. Possibly the physical condition which necessitated the drug in the first instance is still in existence. That type of patient would do very well on ambulatory treatment with a supply of narcotics given to them. That was the type of person to whom I referred. Other than that, the drug addict is abnormal only in the fact that he has terrific difficulty in exerting the will power necessary to do away with this terrible addiction.
So far as treatment is concerned, an argument may arise whether it would be better to have ambulatory or institutional treatment. I hold that institutional treatment would be better if you had the institutions capable of handling these people. One must realize that, having become addicts, they are really ill, and sometimes when they are thrown into jail and subjected to sudden withdrawal of the drug they go through the tortures of the

The bill has given rise to this discussion although I think it was primarily meant to deal with the traffic in illicit drugs.

I want to say a word on clause 3 with regard to penalties for trafficking. It seems to me we have had some interesting discussion here today about the necessity for institutional treatment of people who are addicts. I feel that in any enlightened society there should be every sympathy for the victims of the drug addiction habit. If anything, this bill errs on the side of leniency for the people who are guilty of trafficking in drugs.
I do not know, Mr. Chairman, whether in any civilized society the community is justified in retaining the death penalty. But if we are justified in any respect in retaining the death penalty for murder, for treason or for assisting an enemy-not long ago we passed a bill making it an offence to assist an enemy even with whom we are not at war- in my opinion the trafficker in drugs should be liable to the extreme penalty. The same is true of the person who deliberately organizes the sale of narcotic drugs. He is not only a traitor to his country, but he is a wholesale murderer. If anything is clear it is the fact that the victims of this drug habit are destroyed in their entire personality; they are destroyed physically; they are destroyed spiritually; and they are destroyed as human beings. In my opinion, as long as we are going to retain the death penalty, we should impose the death penalty upon traffickers in drugs.
Could you inform me, Mr. Chairman, whether we are considering clause 2 or clause 3?

In speaking on clause 4, Mr. Chairman, I should like to touch merely on that part of the narcotic drug act that has to do with the administration of this act and particularly the part that affects pharmacists in their everyday duties of handling narcotics and narcotic compounds. In this connection I might say that we prefer the use of the word "pharmacists" rather than the word "druggists" as set out in this bill. The word "pharmacists" is naturally the proper one inasmuch as the faculty in the University of Toronto is the faculty of pharmacy and students graduate with the degree of pharmaceutical chemist, pharmaceutical bachelor and so on. At no time does the word "druggist" enter into that particular faculty. I should like to draw to the attention of the department the fact that "pharmacists" should be used in the hope this will be corrected

at some later time. I think there is a suggestion that the word "druggist" will be altered in the act and the word "pharmacist" used.
The portion of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act about which I was going to speak is the result of the fine co-operation between this department and the various pharmacist groups, particularly in the province of Ontario. I had the privilege of serving on a number of these, and the regulations that have been brought about by these co-operative meetings have been very much appreciated by the pharmacists. There were certain regulations and alleviations for which we asked. These were very thoroughly considered; and I might say that practically all the regulations have been written into this bill. In fact, the department has gone even farther and given us concessions for which we had not asked. I feel that this shows sound administration of what we believe is good legislation.
As you are probably aware, the pharmacists are the custodians of the larger stock of these drugs in their stores where they are kept under lock and key, according to regulations, for use when a prescription authorizing their use is received. When this order, or prescription, is received we are perfectly at liberty to dispense it, ascertaining, of course, that it is properly signed and dated by the prescribing physician.
Under the new regulations, which I would like to speak about particularly, some alleviation of the act is suggested which will be a great help to the public, the physician, and the pharmacist. It must be understood, of course, that the medication prescribed would be in the nature of narcotic compounds and not the straight narcotics as we know them. In other words, a written prescription is necessary for what we call the heavy narcotics such as morphine, cocaine, demerol and heroin. The act has not been changed with respect to them, and we will continue to handle them in the same way. These narcotic compounds are made up largely of codeine and in some cases heroin composition, and are used mainly in the relief of pain and coughs.
The regulations are not altered in respect to the straight narcotics which must be written by a physician and dated before being dispensed. But in the case of codeine compounds, and the like, the amendment suggests that an oral order can be acted upon and the prescription written and signed by the pharmacist receiving the order. I would draw particular attention to the word "oral". The onus, of course, is on the pharmacist to ascertain that he is talking to the licensed
1, 1954
Opium and Narcotic Drug Act prescriber, in each case a doctor, before he can deliver this preparation to a patient. The advantage of this procedure can be easily illustrated and will hasten medication to a legitimate patient at all times. Suppose, after office hours, a physician is contacted at home or elsewhere by a patient for relief of a complaint for which medication containing a narcotic compound would be effective: the physician can call a pharmacy and in a very short time the patient receives the medication so prescribed. The medication, of course, must be compounded with two or more other ingredients in therapeutic doses, and cannot be for hypodermic administration.
How many of us, for example, have received a bottle of cough mixture from a physician and on returning the empty bottle to the pharmacy for a refill have been told that it cannot be done without a new prescription from your doctor. This would entail another visit to your family physician to receive a new piece of paper authorizing the pharmacist to renew this medication. Under the new amendments, the physician could be contacted by phone and, if he felt it should be repeated, the order could be given at that time, to the pharmacist. It is indeed an improvement in service to the patient and certainly less trying on the feelings of both the patient and the physician.
As for the increase in penalties for unlawful trafficking in narcotics, I will leave this to the exponents of the bill, as we pharmacists are not concerned in this phase of the act. We have our rules and regulations to live up to, and our end of the act is being carefully adhered to.
