He said: Mr. Speaker, the measure to be introduced to the house at this time is one which, I think, will be marked by a singular approach to unanimity. Few groups of disadvantaged persons in Canada today command the interest and sympathy of the general public to an extent comparable to the disabled, and any measure which seeks to aid constructively those who are permanently and totally disabled is bound to attract the support of all sections of Canadian opinion. I am sure that what I have said is true of all political groups represented in this chamber and you will therefore, Mr. Speaker, readily appreciate the feeling of personal satisfaction which it gives me at this time to be the minister responsible for introducing one more in a series of important social welfare measures by which this government has built up through the years a comprehensive program of social security in a responsible way for the people of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES- AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Haven't you one good word to say for parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES- AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am sure that almost every hon. member present has had some personal experience within his own family circle, or within the immediate circle of his friends or acquaintances, which will point up the terrible tragedy which invalidity or disability inflicts on the stricken individual and his family. Certainly all of us who represent the people of Canada in this house have personal knowledge of families in our constituencies who have borne unflinchingly through the years the heavy burden of caring for some disabled family member. In thousands of homes across this country Canadian families continue from day to day to carry this heavy burden of responsibility. Most of them carry it without complaint. Only those who have lived in daily contact with such distressing helplessness can fully appreciate the physical, financial and mental strain it can place not only on the helpless individual himself but on all the members of the family group.
To see a young man or a young woman in the full vigour of youth stricken suddenly with some heart-rending disability is a tragedy whose burden can never be fully lifted from the shoulders of those families on whom misfortune falls. Though we, the fortunate and healthy members in society, can do so little to help relieve a tragedy of this kind, and although medical science with all its miraculous accomplishments cannot as yet unlock the secrets of these disabling conditions, we can at least by this measure agree to share some part of the financial burden of caring for the afflicted member.
If we cannot help to ease the mental strain or share the physical burden of care, we can do something to alleviate the financial distress that comes from loss of earning, and to assist in meeting the added financial costs occasioned by invalidity, to ease the pinch of poverty in the home where lack of means accentuates the burden of total and permanent disability.
The measure, Mr. Speaker, now before the house seeks to achieve some part of that objective. It will bring some financial relief to thousands of individuals, and to thousands of harassed, distraught and overburdened families, weighed down with the constant load of caring, day and night, for some helpless loved one.
More than that, through the stimulus which it will give to rehabilitation measures for those who are disabled, this program of disability allowances will bring new hope, new comfort, and new confidence to many others who can be cured but who, failing

Disabled Persons-Allowances
early rehabilitation, face only a future of increasing helplessness and bleak despair. By turning the spotlight of enlightened and progressive legislation on this hitherto neglected area of social need, we shall achieve increasingly from year to year our twofold purpose of successful rehabilitation to lives of greater usefulness for large numbers of disabled persons and, no less important, a measure of comfort and security for the most helpless of our fellow citizens, the totally and permanently disabled whose welfare is this present legislation's principal concern.
When I spoke briefly on the resolution stage I referred to the interest of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in this matter, and I am glad to see him in the house at this time. I would say to him that I am sure all parties will recognize that this measure is due to a large extent to his initiative. I also want to pay my tribute to hon. members on all sides of this house, notably the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand), the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), who moved resolutions from year to year urging the house to give this matter the consideration which we are privileged at this time to give.
I should also mention the part that has been played by a number of provincial governments in making the early enactment of this legislation possible. Three provinces have already passed legislation to provide assistance to disabled persons. Newfoundland passed their dependents allowances act in 1949, Ontario passed their disability pensions act in 1952 and Alberta passed their disability pensions act in 1953.
In the case of Ontario and Alberta, it is perhaps fair to remind the house that when the federal government announced its intention of taking over responsibility for old age security for people of 70 and over, the premier of Ontario indicated that, as a result, that province would be able to save several millions of dollars and he hoped that his province would be able to bring in the measure which is now on the statute books of the province of Ontario.
Since the announcement of the government's intention in the speech from the throne to enact disability allowances legislation at this present session, five other provincial governments have already passed the necessary enabling legislation. Those governments are British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan. Therefore, eight out of ten Canadian provinces are now ready to take advantage of the federal government's offer of assistance in this
field. There have been no official indications as yet from the provinces of Quebec and Prince Edward Island as to their intentions, but I am confident that all the provinces will wish to take the earliest possible advantage of this offer of federal aid and make this program applicable to their respective jurisdictions. Certainly I have no reason to think from the recent dominion-provincial conference that it is not the intention of every government in this country to take advantage of the legislation the second reading of which I have the honour and privilege of introducing at this time.
This program which we are considering today is but the latest in a series of what I think are responsible, humanitarian measures introduced by the federal government during the past fifteen years to improve the social and health conditions of the people of Canada. As I indicated yesterday when I resisted a motion dealing with a proposed increase in one phase of social security, the action which I was taking then was in part predicated upon a desire to see realized other important and, I think, desirable social measures in Canada. When I refer to the progress of the last fifteen years I have in mind the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940; the Family Allowances Act of 1944; the veterans charter; the national health program of 1948 whose significance, I think- and I accept responsibility for this-has not yet made its impression on the people of this country or, I think, on parliament; the Old Age Security Act of 1951; and the old age assistance and blind persons enactments passed in the same year. Hence we can refer to this new measure as another step in an extremely important program of responsible action taken to provide our people with those social welfare measures which, within our capacity, we feel we can from time to time provide.
At this point I should like to outline briefly the main features of this bill, the purpose of which is to provide a nation-wide system of disability allowances. As the house will recall, this measure was forecast in the speech from the throne. The proposed legislation authorizes the payment of $40 a month to needy persons 18 years of age and over who are totally and permanently disabled. I may say that the measure now before us represents the common denominator of agreement which it was possible to reach at the recent dominion-provincial conference on this matter.
The costs of the payments to be provided under this legislation, like old age assistance payments, will be shared equally by the federal and provincial governments. This

Disabled Persons-Allowances will require enabling legislation on the part of each of the participating provinces, and the bill makes provision for agreements to be negotiated by the federal government with each of the provinces concerned. If all of the provinces join in this program it is estimated that from 25,000 to 35,000 disabled Canadians will benefit. The total annual cost will run between $12 million and $16 million, with the federal share of this amount estimated at $6 million to $8 million annually.
In its general outlines, as many members of the house who have examined the context of this bill will recognize, the wording of the new legislation closely parallels that of the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act, both of which received the unanimous approval of parliament in June of 1951. In nine of the thirteen sections of the bill the wording is in fact identical with that of the Old Age Assistance Act except, of course, for the references to "disabled persons" and the use of the term "allowances" instead of "assistance" to describe the payments which will be made.
The four sections of the bill containing features differing in some respects from earlier legislation of a similar kind are sections 3, 7, 11 and 13 of the bill. Most of the points connected with those sections can best be discussed, of course, when we reach the committee stage of the bill but I might perhaps draw special attention at this stage to the following matters.
The maximum amount of the allowance is set at $40 monthly to correspond with existing provisions in Ontario's and Alberta's legislation providing for disability pensions. This amount corresponds also to the provisions of the federal Old Age Security Act, Old Age Assistance Act and Blind Persons Act. The age of eligibility is set at 18 years, the same as in the disability legislation provided for in the province of Ontario. In the province of Alberta the age of eligibility is 21. To meet the concern of certain provinces, some of whom may wish to set a slightly higher age of eligibility, we have provided in section 7 of the bill that any province may, by its own law, designate a higher minimum age if it considers it necessary to do so.
With regard to the amount of $40 I may say all of the provinces thought that was the proper amount and it represents an amount beyond which they were not prepared to go. The residence requirement is set at 10 years, the same as in Ontario's and Alberta's legislation and also in the federal Blind Persons Act.
The income ceilings provided for are the same as those in the federal Old Age Assistance Act and represent the most common wish of the provinces when they were assembled in conference with us here a few months ago. These income ceilings are generally in accordance, therefore, with the preferences expressed by the provinces when we met together.
Provision is made, as is usual in legislation of this character, for the avoidance of duplication between benefits payable under this legislation and comparable benefits paid under other enactments such as the federal Blind Persons Act, Old Age Assistance Act, Old Age Security Act, War Veterans Allowance Act and provincial mothers' allowances laws. Provision is also made, following the precedent established in provincial laws already in effect, for the avoidance of duplication between benefits payable under this legislation and care or maintenance already being provided in institutions of various kinds.
The bill provides for the definition of total and permanent disability to be prescribed by regulation. The definition of this expression "permanently and totally disabled" is, of *course-as was noted the other night by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair)-a highly complicated and difficult one. In framing a definition for our purposes, we will draw heavily on the experience of other countries with similar legislation, as well as that of the provinces which presently administer such programs. But even so, the definition will be subject to change and adjustment in the light of our experience as we gain it from year to year. That is why it is proposed, just as in the definition of "blindness" in the Blind Persons Act, to prescribe in the regulations, rather than in the act itself, for "permanent and total disability" to be defined.
I may add that in our department we have done considerable preparatory work on the drafting of a suitable definition, on the basis of our consultations with representatives of the Canadian Medical Association and the senior health and welfare officers of the ten provincial governments. This matter has also been discussed during the past week at the meeting of the Dominion Council of Health, where all provincial deputies were present; and the definition there formulated will go forward for consideration and, we hope, approval by the conference with the provinces which will be called, following the passage of this legislation, for the drafting of the regulations. What we have in mind in the use of this phrase is a definition that will
[Mr. Martln.l

provide that an applicant must be permanently disabled in the sense that his disability cannot be corrected within the foreseeable future, and he must also be totally disabled in the sense that because of his disability he cannot carry out the ordinary activities of daily living and self-care.
I come now to a very important phase of this whole program, and one that is not related to benefits. That is the very important matter of rehabilitation. There are many in this country, social workers and people who are interested in social matters generally, who believe that we are a little premature in bringing in at this time a nationwide system of disability allowances because they feel that not sufficient has been done in the field of rehabilitation. However, we have given this matter our best attention and we feel that this is the appropriate moment to take the step that we are now taking.
So I come now to the matter that provides the background of this whole problem of disability. I have said that the people of Canada have always felt a special bond of sympathy for their disabled and handicapped fellow citizens. Prominent among these have been the blind, the deaf, the paraplegics, the amputees, those suffering from serious heart conditions or arthritis in seriously disabling form, and, in more recent years, the victims of multiple or disseminated sclerosis, muscular atrophy or dystrophy and other countless long-term ailments. Many of these permanent disabilities arose from illnesses for which medical science has not yet found the answer. Others result from accidents which strike with startling suddenness and in an instant maim and cripple able and healthy bodies.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) brought a case to my attention only the day before yesterday that comes within this very classification, and the fact that we will be able to give rehabilitation services for that particular case, removed thousands of miles from the locale of the particular individual, points out the importance of what I am now seeking to say by way of background of this whole measure. In Canada, as in other countries, we have acted in many ways to meet the social and economic problems faced by a good number of these various disabled groups.
Since 1944, when the province of'Ontario passed the first Canadian workmen's compensation act, provision has been made for payments to the victims of industrial accident and disease. Now all ten provinces have
Disabled Persons-Allowances legislation of this kind. In some of these provinces extensive programs of medical and physical rehabilitation have been developed, their purpose being to restore the injured workman to the full physical capacity and work ability which he enjoyed before his accident. If this cannot be entirely accomplished, everything possible is done to restore him to maximum capacity and to enable him to resume an active, useful life.
These rehabilitation measures in the field of industrial accidents have not been developed on a mere humanitarian basis, however justifiable that may be. Rehabilitation measures have proved to be a matter of plain dollars and cents. Successful restoration of work capacity in the case of injured workmen means a direct saving in pension or compensation payments. Experience has shown that every dollar spent on rehabilitation means a saving of several dollars in compensation awards. Out of this has developed the twofold approach to the problem of disability, with emphasis laid first of all on active treatment and rehabilitation measures, while compensation payments provide for those whose disabilities are more serious or permanent in nature.
The workmen's compensation field is not the only one to apply successfully this twofold principle of rehabilitation and compensation or pension payments. Since the end of the first world war similar provision has been made on a comprehensive scale, as we in this house all know, for our disabled ex-servicemen. Tens of thousands of disabled Canadian veterans have received treatment and rehabilitation services in veterans hospitals to restore them to the fullest possible measure of employability and usefulness in civilian life.
This program has been an outstandingly successful one. Thousands of veterans, as a result of the treatment and rehabilitation services provided through the Department of Veterans Affairs, have had their disabilities brought under control and have returned fit to their normal occupations. Thousands of others have equipped themselves, through carefully managed retraining programs, for new occupations in which they have made successful readjustment of their lives and careers as self-supporting Canadians.
The importance of this in terms of improved morale, the preservation of independence and self-respect, cannot be underestimated. No one can fail to realize the economic and social gain for our country as a whole in the restoration to useful productive employment of tens of thousands of Canadian ex-servicemen.

Disabled Persons-Allowances
What we now propose to do is to apply the lessons learned in respect of industrial accidents and war service disabilities to the benefit of our fellow citizens who suffer similar physical impairments and disabilities which cannot be attributed to war services or the hazards of industrial accident. Here, too, we have another example of what can be accomplished in dealing with the problem of specialized kinds of disability through this twofold approach of rehabilitation and maintenance payments, for we have been operating this twofold program for two decades now in respect of the blind. Since 1937 we have made special provision through blindness allowances for our fellow citizens who have lost their sight. Throughout this entire period, and indeed for a decade or more before, we have had this blind pensions program supported and reinforced by one of the outstanding rehabilitation programs to be found anywhere in the world today. I refer to the program carried on under the auspices of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. This outstanding organization has earned for itself and for Canada a well-deserved reputation throughout the civilized world and has given us inspiration, leadership and experience for the measure which is now receiving second reading.
The C.N.I.B. operates a model rehabilitation program for the 20,000 to 25,000 blind citizens of Canada, a program of great variety, flexibility and versatility. It provides skilled educational and welfare services through its visiting teachers and field workers. It arranges medical care and treatment, including operative surgery for eye conditions. It operates its own blind workshops and home industries. It provides employment for many persons and finds employment for hundreds of others. In short, it provides all the constructive, preventive and therapeutic services which have come to be recognized as the necessary foundation and prerequisite for a program of disability allowances.
Not only the blind but the disabled of all kinds in Canada owe a great deal to the pathfinding services of this institute throughout these past thirty years. The other day the government of Canada was pleased to make a substantial grant toward the building of its new headquarters in Toronto and, as the house knows, annually in the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare a grant for operational services is made to the Canadian National Institute for the Blind.
The preparatory steps leading to the extension of this twofold program have now been taken in the course of these last few years. Six years ago last month, to strengthen and


support the work being done by provincial agencies and by the voluntary groups, the federal government introduced a program of federal health grants amounting to some $35 million a year. At that time one of these grants was specifically earmarked for the development of services for crippled children. This grant has been used to assist the provinces in developing long-range programs for the prevention and correction of crippling conditions in children; to undertake more complete surveys to discover children in need of care; and to develop treatment clinics for the treatment of the cerebral palsy, hitherto one of Canada's most neglected health problems. It has been possible to take advantage of the financial assistance afforded by these grants to extend in many directions the possibilities of successful rehabilitation for thousands of disabled persons.
Other grants included in the national health program have been used, as the house knows, for the construction of hospitals for sick children, the provision of more adequate facilities for those handicapped by tuberculosis and other major diseases, and to stimulate research into these and related health problems. A substantial portion of the federal moneys available to the provinces has been used for the purchase of special therapeutic equipment used in the treatment of disability and for the training and employment of specially qualified health workers for provincial and local services.
Three years ago, in order to give added emphasis to the development of more adequate services for the rehabilitation of the disabled, a national conference on the rehabilitation of handicapped persons was jointly convened in Toronto by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) and myself. This conference led to the establishment of a national advisory committee on rehabilitation, to the creation of a special division within the Department of Labour to coordinate rehabilitation activities in Canada, to the appointment of a national co-ordinator of rehabilitation, and finally to the inauguration of a special program of federal grants in aid to assist the provinces in meeting the costs of a well-balanced rehabilitation program.
Eight provinces have now entered into agreements with the federal government covering those aspects of the program which are of direct concern to the Department of Labour-co-ordination, vocational training, and so on. Co-ordinators of rehabilitation have been appointed in most provinces. Special provision has been made under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act for

training programs for the handicapped. In respect of the health aspects of rehabilitation, a new grant for medical rehabilitation was introduced last year as part of the national health program. This grant, supplementing the crippled children's grant of $500,000 which has been made available since 1948, provided an additional $500,000 in 1953-54 for medical rehabilitation projects to be undertaken by provincial health authorities. For 1954-55, the grant is increased to $1 million annually, available on a pro rata basis to all the provinces.
I should like to give one example of what this rehabilitation means. We entered into an arrangement four years ago with certain provinces. We are now prepared to enter into an arrangement with all the provinces for rehabilitation of persons in receipt of blind pensions. Out of 120 cases of individuals who had been receiving for some period of time blindness allowances or blind pensions under the old act, we were able under this program of rehabilitation, with surgical and medical assistance, to achieve a substantial restoration of vision for 86 of those individuals. That is an indication of what this kind of program is intended to do. I may say frankly that I have felt, during the last four or five years, that I have not properly brought home to the members of this house the significance of this work. There have been criticisms, I do not say in this house but in the press, about some of the expenditures we are incurring. If it were only possible to indicate the positive results, I am sure that much of this criticism about expenditures in the field of health and welfare would be arrested, or at least there would be occasion to discipline some of the references that have from time to time been made about the Department of National Health and Welfare.
It will be seen that the groundwork has been carefully laid, during these past few years, for the establishment of those all-important preventive, treatment and restorative services which constitute the indispensable cornerstone upon which any responsible system of disability allowances must be based. Until the foundations of this complex, manysided rehabilitation program had been laid, no program of pensions or allowances could safely be undertaken. On the solid basis provided by these rehabilitation measures, the legislation now before the house is designed to provide a measure of needed economic security to thousands of our fellow Canadians whose hopes of restoration to useful productive lives cannot be realized through these rehabilitation measures, however skilful and successful they may prove to be.
Disabled Persons-Allowances
So, Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this measure, I would emphasize again that this present legislation is based, not on my authorship but on the example of others. I must say the real idea belongs to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). He made this offer, as I suggested the other night, within a week of the holding of the last election. I mention that to indicate that I hope no one will say this represents an attempt to justify political promises made, because there were none made. This represents a sincere attempt, in co-operation with the provinces, to supply another important development in what we hope is a responsible system of social security in this country. I have the great honour, without hesitation, of recommending this measure to this house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES- AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, the house will approve of the measure brought forward to deal with disabled people. This is something for which we have waited a long time. I can recall that at different times private members' resolutions were introduced advocating this type of legislation when every person in the house thought something should be done about the people who were permanently disabled. I recall speaking on this subject the last time a private member's resolution concerning it was before the house, and describing the lack of something to deal with the totally disabled as a gap in our system of social legislation.
I am glad that this bill has been introduced because from time to time over the past year I have been receiving letters from parents, possibly those who were getting along in years and who had some disabled children, wondering what would happen to those children if the parents were to leave this world or to grow too old to care for the children. I pay tribute at this time to the work that has been done by the service clubs throughout Canada in the matter of totally disabled or crippled children. I am well acquainted with that work because there is a camp supported by service clubs in this area at Merry-wood on the Rideau. From time to time in the summer I visit that camp. I see the work that is being done, and it is a wonderful institution.
I know 'also of the work that is being done by service clubs going into areas and bringing out people who have been disabled, especially children, in order that something may be done through medical or surgical science to overcome their disabilities. On the whole I wish to pay tribute to those people for the great work they are doing. While the minister did make some mention of this point, I would have been better pleased if the bill
5330	HOUSE OF
Disabled Persons-Allowances presented to us today had given us some indication of the meaning of the expression "totally and permanently disabled".
I have before me the definition put out by the department of public welfare in Ontario. In this publication that department states the meaning of "totally and permanently disabled". I should like to quote from this publication because I believe it is the crux of the whole problem, and I am sorry that it has been left out of the bill and is to be dealt with later by order in council. The pamphlet puts this question:
Who is a permanently and totally disabled person?
And the answer is as follows:
One whose disability cannot be corrected within the foreseeable future and who is totally disabled in the sense that he cannot perform the ordinary activities of daily living without the assistance of another person.
This is going to be a most difficult matter to deal with in legislation of the kind before us. I realize the difficulty faced by those who administer the act in Ontario, because I know that on some occasions applications have been brought to me concerning the admission of certain persons for pension purposes.
I have no doubt that applications would be dealt with by a board, and that on the board there would be medical advisers. However, I do wish to bring to the attention of the house the fact that when a disabled person gets a doctor's certificate describing his illness, a most accurate description or pen picture of that illness is of great importance. The board cannot bring all these people before them to discuss their applications, and for that reason this matter becomes even more important.
In the discussion on the private member's resolution last year I quoted the definitions used in various states in the United States in describing those who are eligible for such pensions. I was amazed to find that I was able to quote twelve definitions of what constituted a totally and permanently disabled person. We must realize also that there are people who to all intents and purposes are totally disabled but who, due to rehabilitation or to the fact that they have received some training, are still able to carry on and do a useful job in society.
From time to time this bill will affect new classes of people, and the whole picture will change as years go by. There are at the moment people who will become eligible under this measure but who could have been rehabilitated years ago. These people have now grown too old to take new training. Due


either to environment or to lack of educational facilities they have never had the opportunity to be trained in occupations in which possibly they could have carried on, had they received such training and education. So that as I say the picture is going to change as the years go by, and the younger people will receive the benefits derived from rehabilitation. For many years however we will have to deal with a class of people who, one might say, have never had the chance of rehabilitation so that they might have used the parts of their bodies which could be used, who have never received educational advantages, or who have suffered because of their environment. The Ontario bill might be accepted as a guide. I would hope that the experience they have had in these last two years the bill has been in force would prove beneficial in the administration of the measure now before us, and in the drafting of additional features.
The minister has referred to the veterans program already in effect in Canada, and has made mention of those who have received the benefits of rehabilitation and who, due to their disabilities, have become entitled to pensions. Then there are the blind, and , various others under workmen's compensation acts who have received pensions and are having the benefits of rehabilitation and corrective procedures in order to make it possible for them again to take their places in the labouring world, so that they may earn their living.
There is one other feature in connection with this bill to which I would draw attention, and that is the matter of additional benefits beyond the $40 a month. While we are very proud to have this provision for $40 a month, may I say in passing that there will be cases of those who are totally disabled and who, under the description contained in the Ontario legislation, could not perform the ordinary activities of daily life without the assistance of some other person. For these there would have to be provision for some form of living assistance. It is particularly difficult for those people who are totally disabled and who require in their daily lives the help of someone else. It may be that in the future some provision will have to be made under this legislation, as has been done in connection with veterans, whereby they will receive extra grants by way of living assistance.
I take some pride in the fact that the province of Ontario has pioneered in this field. I note in this pamphlet that this question is asked:
Are there additional benefits?

It will be noted that the pamphlet takes the form of a questionnaire in order that it may be easily understood. This question of additional benefits is particularly important so far as the provinces are concerned, and the carrying out of their part of the bargain to make disability pensions useful. In reply to the question as to whether there are additional benefits, this answer appears in the pamphlet:
A disabled person eligible for an allowance is entitled to receive medical services and certain medicines without costs in accordance with an agreement between the Ontario Department of Public Welfare and the Ontario Medical Association.
To my mind that is a very important consideration, in the matter of additional grants, and I would hope that every province would follow along this line so that these people may receive medical treatment. We know that many of these disabled persons are chronic invalids requiring care and, as is pointed out in the pamphlet, they require certain medicines and additional treatment to an even greater extent than some others who are suffering from a chronic disability. The question of amount, therefore, becomes important. However, if medical care and certain medicines are granted by the province, they will be of marked assistance to these people.
I remember very well the representations placed before members of the House of Commons over quite a number of years. I believe we heard them on four or five occasions, and I recall listening to the representations made by members of that society of disabled persons. I am sure that any member who listened to what they said, and pictured their condition, these disabled persons who came here in wheelchairs and otherwise from all parts of Canada, will approve of this bill.
This measure, one of the more recent links in the chain of social security measures, does not come any too soon; because when I interviewed those people I felt something should be done for them immediately.
So far as this bill is concerned, there is a gap between the ages of 16 when family allowances end and 18 when disabled payments begin. This may be something for study in the future to further the interests of the disabled. During this two-year period the disabled people will receive no money. I wonder whether we can further our program by training the children by way of education. At the present time the service clubs are carrying the brunt of the cost of treatment. If these little children, who are potential invalids, could have corrective measures carried out in their early years, in many cases 83276-337J
Disabled Persons-Allowances there would be no need for the introduction of a bill of this kind. Many of these disabilities could be stopped with early corrective measures.
However, I hail this bill as a forward step. I do know that in the program put forward in the province of Ontario-and I regard Ontario as pioneers in this field-emphasis has been laid on home care. The legislation of that province, as is the case with this bill, does not pay out the money when a particular person is confined to an institution. The disabled person at home qualifies for assistance under the legislation, and that relieves the burden on his friends. The granting of such allowances permits a disabled person to pay his own way and have a certain amount of independence. It will also help out those at home who have the burden of his care.
We shall discuss this bill clause by clause when we are in committee, and we may have something further to say on it. However, I did wish to bring to the attention of the minister-he mentioned it in his speech- the difficulty of defining a totally and permanently disabled person. I do wish that that definition had been placed before the house. I am sorry that it will be determined by order in council.

Mr. Speaker, I have the answer to that, but I am going to exercise the restraint which I counselled on the minister. I will give him the answer privately later on. I have got it right here.
As I have already indicated, Mr. Speaker, this is a welcome measure, and it fills one
Disabled Persons-Allowances of the gaps in our social security program. The minister himself pointed that out and referred to the fact that this is a gap which needed to be filled. But in that connection may I remind the minister and the government, and may I remind the house, that the special joint committee on old age security which met in 1950, and to which I have had occasion to refer a number of times, because I still look on it as one of the most satisfying committees I ever served on in this house, referred to this lack of pensions for disabled or incurable persons as one of the gaps in our social security program.
But may I also remind those who are interested that on page 104 of the report of that committee, where reference was made to gaps in our social security program, two gaps were named. One of them was the lack of pensions for disabled persons, and the other was the lack of a national health insurance program. I hope the moral of that reference will not be lost on the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) or on the government. The government is proud that it has now taken steps to fill to some extent one of the remaining gaps in our social security program. Let them not delay in taking steps to fill the other gap pinpointed by the committee on old age security in 1950.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the hon. member for Lanark has done well to point out that the crux of this whole bill lies in the definition of permanent and total disability. I appreciate the minister's interjection to the effect that this is something that will have to be worked out with the provinces, but I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Lanark that we should have a better understanding in the bill itself as to what the government has in mind. We have had enough experience around here with matters which are decided by regulation and order in council, after legislation has been passed by both houses of parliament and received royal assent, to know whereof we speak.
I have before me a copy of the very excellent brief on this matter which was presented to the federal government on January 15, 1954, by the Canadian Welfare Council. I am sure the minister is fully familiar with this brief and he will be aware that this whole question of the definition of permanent and total disability is a matter of major concern in the brief of the Canadian Welfare Council. That council points out that in the main there are three groups of disabled persons. First there is that group which is referred to as the hard core of disabled persons, persons who are completely and totally disabled and for whom there is no

Disabled Persons-Allowances hope of any cure whatsoever. For those persons there should not be any question about the allowance that should be available to them, and it should be on as generous a basis as possible.
Then there is the second group who are defined by the Canadian Welfare Council as consisting of people who suffer a disability or a handicap of some sort but who nevertheless are able to work and make their own living to a certain extent. However, they are people who do suffer because of their disability and there is a case in many instances for some assistance to them to compensate for the disability from which they suffer.
Then, says the Canadian Welfare Council, there is a third group which lies in between the other two extremes of disabled persons. This group consists of people who are not totally and permanently disabled but who are disabled to the point that they cannot earn their living, and the fear felt by the Canadian Welfare Council is that these people may lose out completely. They are not capable of obtaining and holding employment to meet their needs. If, on the other hand, they are not totally and permanently disabled how can they qualify for allowances as defined in this legislation? The Canadian Welfare Council holds the fear that unless this matter of the definition of total and permanent disability is cleared up this legislation may induce people to deteriorate rather than encourage them to do everything they can to become rehabilitated. The Canadian Welfare Council puts the case very well, I think, when it states in its brief:
Under such a three-fold plan the need to prove that one was incapable of rehabilitation would be greatly lessened. Maintenance would be provided when needed, by the method appropriate to the degree of handicap produced by the disability.
To sum up: While recognizing the need for disability allowances for totally and permanently disabled persons, we are strongly of the view that such allowances must be thought of in terms of their effect upon those who are not eligible as well as upon those who are eligible for benefit from them.
If I interpret that sentence aright, I think what the Canadian Welfare Council is afraid of is that the kind of definition we now have will make some people who are in that inbetween group feel that the only way in which they can get this allowance is by letting their physical condition deteriorate and their morale go down until they are totally and permanently disabled. When I express this concern I am expressing not only my own reaction and my own concern about this matter but I am quoting from the excellent brief prepared, as I say, by the Canadian Welfare Council. Let me go on and read


the rest of that paragraph from which I was quoting just now. It concludes as follows:
When this is done the need for a broader program becomes at once clearly apparent. Only if disability allowances are made part of a comprehensive plan which provides for the economic needs of all disabled persons can the dangers we have indicated and which are inherent in the single approach be overcome or avoided.
As we proceed with the discussion of this legislation, we on this side of the house will continue to press our contention that we should have a clearer understanding as to what the definition is that people must meet in order to qualify for this allowance. What we are asking for is that it be liberalized. Perhaps I might say, in the language of the Canadian Welfare Council, that we are asking that it be made more intelligent and more appropriate to the needs of these people.
I now move on to say something which the minister knows I will say.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES- AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: I always know what the hon. gentleman will say.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES- AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
I thank the minister for that compliment. I am glad to know that he has been listening to me across the years and that, as time moves on, some of the ideas that are put forward from parties on this side of the house and from outside the house do get into his head.
I suggest strongly and earnestly that the amount of this allowance should be greater than the figure of $40 a month which is proposed in this bill. I suggest that it should be not less than the same figure that I suggested yesterday in another connection, namely that the amount should be not less than $60 a month. I thought of this in particular-although it was my intention on behalf of this group to propose it-when the minister was uttering those extremely flowery and sympathetic words, in the opening part of his remarks, with regard to our concern for disabled people. I suggest that to express that sympathy and that concern with an amount of only $40 a month in this day and age is not good enough. To suggest that we cannot afford the higher amount which we propose is just an alibi. I need not go into that matter. After all, I did so yesterday with respect to my contention that old age and blind pensions should be not less than $60 a month. If we insist that we are an intelligent, modern, Christian civilization we cannot afford not to do a great deal better than to give only $40 a month to the people in our society whom we recognize as deserving pensions of this kind. I argue strongly, and I do so on behalf of this group, that the amount of this allowance should be not less than $60 a month.

I suppose that one of the arguments the minister may want to throw back in response to that suggestion-he says he knows my speech; I may say that I know his answers too-is that there has been an arrangement with the provinces. I am sure that every night when the minister goes to bed he must say "God bless the provinces"; they save him from all sorts of trouble.

speechtext:
My friend the hon. member for Lanark suggests that when he and I think of those on the opposite side at night we find ourselves counting sheep. At any rate, Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare thinks it is an answer to say that the provinces feel that $40 is an appropriate figure, may I point out to him that if they have expressed that view, it is because $20 a month or half of that figure is as much as they feel they can afford in view of their provincial resources.
Our view is that this matter should not be on a 50-50 basis, as is old age assistance, but rather that it should be on a 75-25 basis, 75 federal and 25 provincial, as is the case with the blindness allowance. Surely there is far more relationship between a disability pension and the blindness allowance than there is between a disability pension and old age assistance. If the house will accept our view that it should be on a 75-25 basis rather than on a 50-50 basis it will be seen right away that a $60 pension which I am now suggesting would not be objected to by the provinces because that would require them to pay only $15 out of the $60, leaving $45 to be paid by the federal government.
The minister may ask if I have worked out what that will cost. I may say that I have done so. I have the figures under my hand and when we get into committee, if he is interested, I can go into the matter and again I can relate it, as I did yesterday, to our gross national production and to what is an appropriate portion of our wealth to spend in this way.
I move on, Mr. Speaker, to suggest that after all the fight that we put up to get rid of the means test in respect of old age pensions at 70 years of age and over and after all the appropriate castigating we have done of the means test in relation to items like the war veterans allowance, we are disappointed to find that here the old so-and-so, the means test, turns up again. The government says:	We are
Disabled Persons-Allowances very sympathetic; we are very sorry that there are people in our midst who are disabled, who have incurable diseases they will not get over as long as they live, but our sympathy does not restrain us from imposing the means test on the allowances that we are prepared to give them.
We think there should be no means test on these allowances. If we cannot yet win that point-we will win it some day-I have another suggestion to offer. When I say that we will win it some day, I mean it. I can remember year after year standing up in this house and pleading for the removal of the means test from the old age pension and having some people in this house and outside of it say:	You know, Stanley, that
you are just talking; you are never going to get rid of it. However, we got rid of it. Some day we will get rid of the means test from the war veterans allowance and we will get rid of it from this allowance as well.
In the meantime I suggest that to apply the ceiling levels that are set out in the Old Age Assistance Act is a procedure that is altogether too restrictive. I know that in the case of a married couple where there is blindness on the part of one spouse or the other or in the case of a single person who is blind, the relationship is to the figures set out in the Blind Persons Act. But where blindness does not come into the picture, it is the old age assistance levels of permissible income which have been imported into this act. If the government is not prepared to go all the way at this time, I say that at least they should set a higher figure. I believe that one of the provinces suggested that the ceiling of permissible income might be something of the order of $1,000 single and $1,500 married.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, I make the suggestion of an alternative to removal of the means test in terms which I hope even this government might be prepared to consider.
I agree with the hon. member for Lanark that something should be done about that age gap which is now left between the point at which family allowances are discontinued and that at which it will be possible to receive
5336	HOUSE OF
Disabled Persons-Allowances the allowances under this legislation now before us. That seems to me to be the "most unkindest cut of all".
Here is a government that boasts of its social security program. It has family allowances from the time of birth until the age of 16. It has old age assistance from age 65 to 69, under a means test, which we deplore. It has old age security for everyone 70 years of age and over. It is now providing for disability allowances from age 18 up to the point where one could qualify for old age assistance, but in the case of the person who may be disabled the whole of his life, the child born with an incurable condition, the government has left that little gap between the ages of 16 and 18. If there is an explanation for that I will be surprised.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES- AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Could my hon. friend tell me what Saskatchewan's view was on that very point?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES- AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Saskatchewan and the other provinces had to deal with this matter on the basis proposed by the federal government of a 50-50 split. Saskatchewan had to consider, as did all the other provinces, all these various items in terms of what it would cost them in relation to their provincial revenues. I suggest that Saskatchewan and the other provinces would be quite glad to go further with regard to these various regulations if the government would accept the proposition we lay down, namely, that it should be on a 75-25 split rather than on a 50-50 split. The minister may offer that prayer of thanks for the provinces but he cannot blame everything on them while some of us are here to watch him.
One other criticism I offer with respect to the legislation has to do with the residence clause which requires residence in Canada for not less than ten years. On its face that may seem to be a reasonable requirement, but I ask the minister to face the fact that there will be people entering this country as immigrants who on arrival are in perfectly good health-they have to be because they have to pass the medical examination imposed by the government-and in some instances some of these people will contract incurable diseases after arrival, perchance some of the diseases the minister referred to in his remarks today, or perchance they may suffer some accident which makes them invalids for the rest of their lives before they have been here ten years. We have got to do something for them. Failure to make provision for them in legislation of this kind simply means that the burden is thrown on the provinces or on the municipalities.
tMr. Knowles.]

The various suggestions that I have made spell out my earlier statement that this measure does not go far enough. I hope that even yet we may get improvement with respect to some of these points, particularly with regard to the amount of the allowance, the means test level, the age gap between 16 and 18 and the definition of total permanent disability. Nevertheless, as I have already said, despite my feeling that there are these shortcomings and inadequacies, we are glad to see parliament at last being given a chance to take the step to fill this gap that parliament has wanted to take for a long time. We have had private members' motions introduced frequently and, as I say, the minister played his part in helping to talk them out. But at last the house is getting a measure it has long been ready to support.
Parliament welcomes the opportunity to put legislation of this kind on the statute books. It begins to fill one of the gaps to which the old age security committee referred in 1950. I hope it will not be long until we have the opportunity to fill the other gap, that of national health insurance, so that we might move on to the achievement of an adequate over-all social security program for the people of this country the like of which we have the wealth to afford, the like of which our people, because they produce that wealth, fully deserve.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having participated in innumerable debates when pressure was put on the government to introduce legislation providing payments for disabled persons, it is indeed refreshing to be able to stand up at this time and offer our support for the principle of the bill now before us. I had rather hoped that no sour note would be injected into the debate, but on the other hand I believe that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was quite justified in complaining, shall I say, about the fact that the minister had obviously overlooked-

During most of the years I have been in the House of Commons I have urged the government to give favourable consideration to the question of payments to our disabled Canadians. While I felt at times that maybe our efforts were a bit futile, I never lost hope. I am a confirmed optimist, but since the spring of 1950 my hopes have been much higher than at any previous time. I had the opportunity of serving as a member of the old age security 83276-338

Disabled Persons-Allowances committee. I realize how frequently the various delegations that appeared before the committee made reference to this matter even though it was not actually included in our terms of reference.
I realize, too, and I believe I pointed this out last year in the course of my remarks on a private member's resolution relating to disabled persons, that our committee saw fit to refer to this matter, even though I repeat it could not under those terms of reference actually make recommendations with respect to the matter.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to page 103 of the evidence of the old age security committee, dated June 28, 1950. I note also that on page 103, under other claims to priority, it states:
Finally, in its study of the old age security systems in effect in other countries, and in its consideration of the evidence presented by representative Canadian organizations and individuals, the committee has had to keep constantly in mind the place of old age in an over-all security program. While the terms of reference of the committee have limited its study to the specific field of old age security, it has not felt it advisable to overlook the fact that there are other areas of social need in which governments, both provincial and federal, may be called upon to take in the future a substantial measure of responsibility.
Then again on page 101 there is a brief reference to this matter under the heading of "premature ageing and invalidity." This makes specific reference, of course, to disabled persons, and I quote:
The reverse of the problem of retaining older workers in the labour market is that presented by the prematurely aged and invalids who are obliged to retire from employment before their normal time. The committee has been deeply impressed by the evidence presented as to the position in which invalids and incurables find themselves at present. It has also received representations from organizations representing the blind, and blindness is. of course, part of the total problem of invalidity. The committee has felt, however, that the terms of reference established for it ruled out the possibility of a detailed examination of this problem as it applies to the younger age group.
I am going to make a reference to something, Mr. Speaker, that I have not mentioned during the past four years. A moment ago I stated that because of representations made to our old age security committee, and because of the feelings of the members of that committee with respect to this question of invalidity, my hopes were buoyed up. There was another reason for it. I hope the minister will not mind my mentioning this, and he will understand why I have never mentioned it during the last four years. He may recall that while our committee was sitting he crossed the floor one day and sat with me. We were discussing the work of the committee and the possible recommendations of
5338	HOUSE OF
Disabled Persons-Allowances the committee. He said something to this effect: We must not at any time forget that very important class of people, the invalids or those who are permanently disabled. He said something must be done for them. Now, these might not be the exact words, and I have never mentioned that until this day because I would consider it unfair to have done so during the discussion of any private member's resolution or anything I might have sponsored myself. However now the legislation is before us I think it is fair to mention it. I wish to compliment the minister upon having now reached that stage where the feelings which he indicated he held in the spring of 1950 have become a matter of direct action through the introduction of the bill before us.
I cannot, of course, overlook the emphasis the minister laid upon this question of rehabilitation services. I well recall that the Canadian Association of Incurables constantly repeated the following views: First, pensions or payments are definitely required because so many of our disabled persons are so handicapped they cannot earn even a single dollar. There is another thought that comes to me just at this point. I remember, too, they said so many people will not hire individuals who are physically handicapped simply because the public very often will not accept these people.
I recall one case and I believe this man was one of the delegates. He held a job as an elevator operator in a building. He said he had to sit in the wheel chair while operating the elevator, but he could do it quite satisfactorily from the mechanical point of view. One person who was in the habit of using that elevator actually served notice that unless they secured another elevator operator he was not going into that building. I am certainly underlining the fact that that is not the general feeling among Canadian people.
I believe there is a responsibility upon the Canadian people today to do everything within their power to assist these persons to rehabilitate themselves. I feel there is a great field there where the government might quite properly function.
I know, too, the service clubs and other organizations have been doing a great deal in this particular field. I am extremely happy to know that while payments are to be made to the permanently disabled, this question of rehabilitation is being given the utmost consideration.
This reference to the definition of disabled persons is one which rather intrigues me. I presume that when the conference was held a reference was made to the definition of disabled persons in the Alberta act. I am


not saying it is a good one, but I do want to point out a problem with which I know they were confronted in this connection. According to the bill which was assented to on March 31, 1953 in the Alberta legislature, a disabled person was defined as a person who is suffering from a chronic disability and is physically unfit for gainful employment. Then, the two words "chronic disability" are defined. They mean a disability from which a person has suffered for a period of twelve months or longer.
While I realize that this matter of the definition is not in the bill before us but will be a matter of regulation, I still suggest to the minister that if any degree of agreement has been reached thus far, and I think probably it must have been discussed with the representatives of the provinces, he might give us some information on this point. Here is a problem with which Alberta was confronted in connection with the definition. A person may be partially a mental case and partially physically disabled. The mental condition is not so serious as to warrant the placing of the individual in an institution or mental hospital. I recall one case specifically. The person in question was a female, about 30 years of age. When she was less than a year old she suffered paralysis. I guess it was the old infantile paralysis to which we used to refer. It affected her mind. It is true that today under very close and careful supervision she might be able physically to do a certain amount of work, yet there is this mental condition. I presume her mental age would be around 9 or 10.
Under the Alberta act as we knew it prior to this year, that person would almost invariably be characterized as suffering from a mental disability and therefore prohibited from security benefits under the disabled persons act. The situation became so common that finally in the last session of the provincial house the act was amended so that those mentally unfit for gainful employment, provided they were not confined to a mental hospital, could qualify under the provisions of the act. I would like to ask the minister if he would comment on that aspect of the bill that is before us.
