Mr. Chairman, in considering these fifty bills there is no hope, of course, that we can give them consideration, because that is not the method of this House of Commons. However I should like for a moment to refer to a statement by the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, as it is reported at page 5211 of Hansard for May 28. I am glad the hon. member is in his seat. While I do not intend to be critical of him, I do wish to point out that what he said gave the wrong impression. I am sure the impression he left was unintentional, when he described the attitude of certain of us in the miscellaneous private bills committee, which considered these bills before they were brought to the house. I find at the page indicated that the hon. member is reported to have said:
Every member received copies of the evidence in each of these cases, and if any particular hon. member did not read that evidence then it is his own fault.
I agree with him so far. Then he continued:
The fact is that every one of these bills came before us en bloc and they received unanimous consent of the miscellaneous private bills committee.
Technically, sir, the hon. member may be correct. Although some of us did not vote on these bills at all, I suppose it could be said that by our silence we had given consent since none of us raised his voice against them. But I submit that does not give a true picture of what we had in our minds and hearts in regard to these bills, and particularly the manner in which they are considered in that committee.
Time and again I have raised my voice in the committee on miscellaneous private bills. I see the hon. member for Parkdale in his seat, to whom I pay tribute as a conscientious and courteous chairman. I know he would back up my statement that on almost every occasion the committee met I raised my voice against the procedure followed. I see him smile, and it would seem that he has some recollection of that. I am sure he will also confirm my statement that while I did not say anything at the last meeting of the committee on miscellaneous private bills, I did make my usual protest at the committee which met the week before.
We are now faced with these fifty bills. The hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, is of course a new member, and
[The Deputy Chairman.]
is new on that committee. It can be said that perhaps he does not know our attitude toward the method adopted in considering these bills, particularly the procedure of considering them en bloc, which is exactly the same the committee of the whole house is doing here today. He will understand our criticism of the fact that full consideration is not given to each bill. So much for the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia.
Let us now turn to the bills themselves. There were definite reasons for the fact that we were silent in the standing committee. First of all, it is true that the committee passed these bills. Well, what else could it do with them? I remember very well that when the Prime Minister spoke on this subject he said there was a small minority in Quebec and Newfoundland who needed relief from their marital troubles and that this was the procedure under which they obtained it.
I submit to you, sir, that these fifty people had paid their money-and the evidence has shown in the last few days that it is a considerable amount of money-and had paid it in good faith. They had submitted then-evidence, either true or perjured as the case may be-and I am sure there were some of both-and they were there, generally, to obtain their divorces. Under those circumstances what else could the standing committee do, when it was set up for that particular job? What else can a member who does not believe in the whole procedure do, except protest against that procedure, as I have done on many occasions?
Those of us who object to it could, of course, have held up the procedure of the committee indefinitely, but I suggest to the hon. member for Victoria that he would not want that. We could make a nuisance of ourselves, if necessary, and as we have proved on occasions. We could keep that up indefinitely. But we had a job to do that day, and we did it. I would serve the hon. member notice that if our attitude in that regard is to be misrepresented in the house, then if necessary the struggle in the committee on miscellaneous private bills can be kept up.
I notice that the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, agrees with me in the matter of procedure. As reported at page 5211 he said:
I found out, as did every other hon. member, that I did not like the procedure, and I did not like the evidence I have had to read. I think there is collusion in it.
I know on Friday evening he modified that statement to some extent; but his statement is there on the record. When he was challenged for having said that there is collusion, and at

the same time voting for these bills, he modified the statement, and those modifica-cations may be found at page 5212 of Hansard. I submit however that the record stands, and I have quoted from it exactly as it was recorded in the debates. The hon. member is reported to have said:
I did not like the evidence I have had to read. I think there is collusion in it.
Another reason we did not protest as strongly or, shall I say, as often as usual on this particular occasion is that we were informed, and I believe reliably so, that the whole matter of divorce procedure is to be looked over and considered by the procedural committee, a committee from which we have not yet had a report, but of which we still have some hopes. That did not prevent my making vigorous protests on previous occasions the committee met; but it does explain to a degree why we did not press our opposition at every meeting of the committee. As I have said, if our intentions in that regard are misunderstood, then we can make them very clear by protesting every time a bill comes up. I think, myself, that perhaps that would be an exaggerated conclusion to seek; but we do not want any question to be left as to where we stand.
Another reason for our silence in that particular committee was that the committee before which these fifty bills were placed passed them in the course of, roughly, a couple of minutes. I have often timed it with my wrist watch, although I did not on this occasion. One reason we did not block any of the bills, or did not bother particularly with that committee, was that none of these bills had been contested, whereas there were two others to come up which had been. There were four lawyers in the room, two on each case, and sitting outside were the witnesses in both cases who were waiting in case it might be decided to call them. They were sitting there waiting in case it might be the decision of the committee to have them called. Naturally, we were expecting that we would have to spend a considerable time on these two cases which were contested, and that proved to be the fact, because we had two meetings of the committee on that day, and it took most of our spare time on that day to go over these two cases. We wanted to give those cases which were contested a very close scrutiny. In those cases there was the probability of an injustice being done on one side, and if there was we wanted to know about it.
In the meantime these two particular cases have become history, as it were, and since they are not before us I cannot make definite references to them today, although I am still in doubt as to who was responsible for that
Private Bills-Divorce
one particular case being withdrawn. It is true that at that time we made a recommendation that, since the lawyer for the petitioner had withdrawn the case, it be sent back to the other place with the suggestion that they could now take whatever action they considered necessary. I do not know what the constitutional problem is in that case. It is the first case of that kind of which I have had any experience. My own idea was that the case was in the hands of this house, and whether or not a lawyer can simply get up and wash his hands of the whole thing because it has been a hoax, and simply withdraw it out of the committee and that is the end of it, I am not sure.

Perhaps I can clear it up for my hon. friend. That bill will be reported with the preamble not carried, and the reasons will be stated. It means that the bill simply will not be carried by this house and therefore an act will not be passed. As to the other reference to the Senate, on the instructions of the committee I simply reported to the chairman of the Senate committee the possibility of perjury, and drew it to his attention. I have had a reply acknowledging that letter.

I thank the hon. member for giving that explanation to the house. He is much better qualified to do that than I am, but at any rate I shall mention those cases no more and return to these particular bills. Both cases were thrown out, of course, as is now well known.
In regard to these particular cases that are in front of us and in regard to other cases like these that may be protested in the future, I should like to serve notice that in such cases they will be seriously considered in the committee, if I remain a member of that committee and can urge that same opinion upon my colleagues. I think it is a good thing that the counsel for these people and the people themselves will know that where there is a protested case and where there is a chance of an injustice having been committed they will also have recourse to the miscellaneous private bills committee, with the assurance that their protests and their appeal, because that is actually what it is, will have serious consideration and a thorough examination in that committee.
I was glad to hear the words of the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia that I have quoted. I was glad to see that he was disturbed at the procedure and the way in which we were handling these fifty bills. I am glad to see some disturbance in the minds of some other members also. I may say that in that there is a sign of progress. In that particular disturbance there is some

Private Bills-Divorce
hope. I may say also that it was not ever thus. Some years ago, in my introduction to this committee the usual procedure was simply to push these bills through the committee en bloc, en masse, forty or fifty of them at a time. Woe betide the committee member who would dare to raise his voice in opposition. I am glad that that situation has to some extent changed. I believe it does show some change of opinion. The cry in those days was, of course, well these bills have been passed by the Senate committee, composed of men with legal and mature minds; they have heard the evidence; they cannot be wrong. Like Brutus, they are honourable men, and so our job in this committee is to simply rubber stamp their decision. Well, sir, the situation has changed and the infallibility of the Senate committee on divorce has been proved a squib which exploded with a loud bang on a recent historic occasion, because I think that occasion was historic.
These fifty bills are an embarrassment to this committee. You can feel it and hear it behind the curtains from any member to whom you wish to speak. The bills are an embarrassment to this committee and to the members of the miscellaneous private bills committee, and I believe they are an embarrassment to this government. Still, I am not going to oppose them. These fifty bills are not contested. Let us pass them and get on to the legislation which is the reason for our presence here. I know I was not elected to listen to the evidence in divorce cases. I am not competent to judge the evidence or to assail it. I want to get on with the work for which I was sent here, and I do not want to spend the rest of my life untangling divorce cases. Let us get on with it now. Let us pass the bills, but let us devise for the future a method by which that embarrassment may be removed for all time from these halls.

I am sorry I cannot agree with my colleague in his last remarks. At least one of these cases was contested, and I have read the evidence since we met here the last time. I would like hon. members to follow with me very briefly the sort of material which may be found in some of these cases. I am not going to mention any names, and 1 am not going to make any references that I could not make in the best circles of society. But there are some investigators in these cases that have appeared frequently, and I cannot understand why information given by investigators of this sort can be accepted and divorces granted. There were three male investigators and one female

investigator on this case. I am referring to evidence that appears in relation to Bill No. 434 which is before us. There were two investigators who swore they went to this particular home some six months ago. The evidence starts out with getting the usual story, but this was a different type of mystery. One man went to the house and he says:
We checked every room in the house.
Q. Did you go into the house?A. Yes, we went into the house.
Q. How did you proceed to get into the house?- A. We proceeded to check the electricity.
Q. You pretended you were going there to check the electricity?-A. Yes, so we checked every room
and Mrs. 

 was showing us every place in the
house.
It seems strange that after a man admits lying for the sake of getting into a house, suddenly everything else he says after that is the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Well, this man was questioned by the lawyer for the respondent, and here are the questions and answers:
Q. I am asking you how many bedrooms are there in that house?-A. I don't know.
Q. How many beds are in the house?-A. Oh, I don't know.
Q. Did you go-?A. I didn't check all the beds.
Q. You went to check the electricity?-A. Yes.
Q. How many switches are there in the apartment?-A. We didn't check the switches.
Q. What were you checking exactly?-A. We checked the room.
Q. You checked the rooms? Well, how many rooms are there, in the home, not only bedrooms, but other rooms in the house, how many rooms are there?-A. I do not remember. I checked that in my notes, the day I checked.
As I read the evidence, Mr. Chairman, it appears to me that one of the investigators did go to the house and made elaborate drawings of bedrooms and furniture. Two women who were in the house swore that there was only one man went, and two men swore that two went. In view of the evidence in the case from one of the men who apparently know so little about what he saw, it would seem to me that probably the women were telling the truth on that particular occasion.
But then there was a ladder that featured in the story. Perhaps I should take a minute to tell the committee the story of this ladder. The case really hinges on what three men saw after climbing up the ladder and looking in an upstairs window, and here is how the evidence goes:
Q. And you mentioned that you were up first?- A. Well, it is a way of talking; I would say the first one. We were going up slowly and sometimes I was putting my foot on his and trying to take a grab of a rung and sometimes I would cross-

I will not dignify these gentlemen by placing their names in Hansard, but call them Mr. Z and so on.
. . . Mr. Z's hand.
Q. But you went up first?-A. I wouldn't say that; sometimes he was maybe a few inches higher than me and sometimes maybe I was higher than him.
Q. Are you telling me that you both went up together side by side?-A. Yes, it is a broad ladder.
Q. How wide is the ladder?-A. It is a big ladder. I don't like to say it is a very tall or long ladder but it is a very wide ladder.
Q. How wide?-A. Maybe two feet.
Q. And the two of you were climbing side by side?-A. Oh yes. We had done that before.
And then the acting chairman came into the discussion and he asked:
Q. I presume, witness, it is a ladder you have for the purpose?-A. Not exactly. We use it a lot many times but it is a handy ladder around. It is a hard ladder. It is a heavy duty ladder.
Q. Is it made of aluminum?-A. No, it is light wood but big wood, and the rungs are strung with some braces under. It is a big ladder and a strong ladder.
The hearing adjourned until 2 p.m.
But Mr. Chairman, that is not the end of the ladder story.
I think it should be.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Let us just have one rung at a time.

I think we should have the end of the ladder story because this is really where the funny part comes in. As I said, there was a lady, we will call her Miss L but I do not know what a lady would be doing out after midnight with this crowd. The evidence continues:
Q. Where was Miss L, during the time of the investigation?-A. She was in my car.
Q. She did not leave the car that night?-A. No.
Now, I want to go into the question of the window. This is the evidence:
Q. On what side of the building was the window in question that you looked into?-A. On the north side.
Now, Mr. Chairman, here is a ladder on the north side of the house and then this lady is questioned by the defence counsel as follows:
Q. On which side?-A. On the south side.
Q. Well, we have been told by Mr. Z and the others that the bedroom in question is on the north side, what would you say as to that?-A. I don't know where the bedroom would be.
Q. So on what side was the ladder put up?-A. I can't say exactly.
Although, Mr. Chairman, the ladder was on the north side and the lady in question was on the south side she was able to see through that house in the dark of night and see three men climb up a ladder, and on the evidence of what these three men saw from that ladder a divorce was granted.
Private Bills-Divorce
I think hon. members of this house had better start taking a look at these 400 divorces which go through each year. I think that the parliament of Canada cannot be a party to having this sort of evidence coming into the other chamber and coming on to us so that we are asked to break up homes on the type of evidence appearing in this report. As I have already said, I probably would not have spoken about the case had it not been for the fact that these particular investigators gave evidence in another case whereby a wealthy man in Montreal was relieved of the responsibility of supporting his wife and young baby, on the same sort of evidence I have quoted here. The evidence of these men was accepted in the other chamber by those who examined them and who apparently said, "These detectives give their information, it must be true". They were prepared to accept the evidence which was given as I have described it by these investigators, three of them men and one woman, and under the circumstances I have described. I would suggest that hon. members should refer this particular case back to the Senate or to our committee on miscellaneous private bills to have another look at it before the members of this chamber put their official seal on it and endorse the sort of evidence submitted in report 383.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Chairman, before you put this to the vote I think the hon. member who spoke before me should be fair. I am informed that in this particular case the Senate committee took evidence for 7J hours and I am quite convinced, although I do not read these cases and I do not intend to read them, that there must be further evidence besides what the hon. member related to the committee. I do not like to see the other place held up to ridicule in all cases and in this one I think the hon. member has not brought out the full evidence.

Mr. Chairman, I have not said anything on the question of divorce for about ten years, but I have been doing a lot of listening and I must admit that I have not heard anything yet, not even from the hon. members of the C.C.F. party, about a method of curing the curse of divorce. What is the cause? That is the question, and we should be far more concerned about that than a method of handling these bills. How many cases of divorce have we taken from the courts? I think we have robbed the courts of some. I think the hon. member for Lanark would agree with me when I say that when

Private Bills-Divorce
young couples get into difficulty through selfishness or something like that they should go to the family doctor or their spiritual adviser instead of a lawyer or the courts.
I know there are those in Canada and the United States who are finding a cure. There are groups of men in different places, lawyers, doctors, ministers, businessmen, and social workers, who have formed committees to investigate every case which looks about hopeless and they have robbed the divorce courts of many cases. I think we could spend the time of this house to far better advantage in finding a cure for divorce instead of trying to prove that the Senate has not been painstaking in its work.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a very few remarks to make. The insinuation has been made that we should not be spending our time on this matter. But I submit, Mr. Chairman, that we should, because what we do when we pass these divorce cases can have very serious consequences. We not only dissolve marriages but we also relieve a goodly number of husbands of the responsibility of supporting their wives and families. Further than that, the effect of our passage of these bills means that we are branding certain people of having been guilty of committing adultery. That, in turn, has the effect in some parts of Canada of robbing these people of the rights of citizenship in a great many respects. I feel that the evidence in a great many of these cases is entirely insufficient. I have had cases called to my attention where there has been all kinds of blackmailing going on after the case had passed the Senate committee, because it was commonly assumed that once a bill had passed the Senate commitee and had been recommended by them that that was the end of the matter, and those who had given false evidence immediately began their habit of blackmailing the people who were vitally concerned.
I have one case in mind where one of the witnesses has had to leave Canada and is now in Mexico. Unfortunately the case was not proceeded with to its final conclusion. My aim was to have this man fetched from Mexico in order to appear before our miscellaneous private bills committee. If we had been able to do as we desired, I think this House of Commons would have received a good illustration of the effect of our passing these divorce cases as if they were just so much unimportant and minor legislation.

Before you put the question again, Mr. Chairman, there are one or two points I should like to make about this matter. I do not want to go into the merits or the moral aspects of divorce. However,

as was mentioned by my friend the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, I would not want the impression to be left that the Senate committee who handle these divorces are not doing what I think is an excellent job. As to the case mentioned by the hon. member on the opposite side who first spoke, I happen to know, as has already been mentioned, that that divorce committee presided over by the chairman who has had some 42 years' experience in legal and judicial matters and composed of four other senators who are tried and true in this type of work, spent 7J hours examining the witnesses whom they had there before them. I do not know whether hon. members know the old court of appeal maxim or not. The court of appeal says that a trial judge who has the witnesses before him is in a much better position than is any court of appeal to decide on the question of perjury; and the general rule is that they will, in almost all cases, take the opinion of the trial judge in that respect. Here we have exactly the same situation. We have the divorce committee that spent 7| hours looking at the witnesses. After the case they went into a two hours' conference with regard to it-the five of them-and after careful deliberation they decided there was sufficient ground for divorce. Then the private bills committee of the House of Commons meets. We have no formal courtroom in which to meet. We have no formal method by which we call witnesses. Questions can be put by anybody at any time to any witness. We have witnesses called into the room indiscriminately. On the whole the procedure is carried on very informally. Generally speaking, I do not think hon. members read the evidence thoroughly and go through all the evidence.
May I ask my hon. friend one simple question? Was any witness in connection with any of these fifty cases with which we are dealing today called before the miscellaneous private bills committee?

Yes; there were some witnesses called before the committee. I did not say that, with due respect to the hon. member. I did not mean to create that impression. We have called witnesses before the committee, of course.

I doubt that the hon. member understood or heard my question. I am asking this straight question. Were any witnesses called before the private bills committee in connection with any of the fifty cases with which we are dealing today?
No.

No. Of course there were not, as there was apparently no dispute raised with regard to the fifty cases that have been mentioned. I am merely trying to point out that we should not lightly disregard the work of the Senate in this matter and hold it up to ridicule, as I think has been done by hon. members opposite in this chamber today.
It is part of their program to abolish the Senate.

I wanted to say this so that that impression would definitely not be left. I know that the divorce cases handled by the Senate are just as efficiently handled as elsewhere. Indeed I think they are better handled than they are by the crowded courts in the supreme court of Ontario. You get a better hearing by the Senate committee because there is more time involved; you get a more convenient time for your hearing and you get a hearing with more dispatch. I think we should put the facts down as they are with regard to this divorce situation. I know that it is an awkward one. I know that some members do not like having to handle this work. Perhaps we should not be doing it. However, 1 have yet to hear a suitable alternative offered by anyone, in my short experience in the House of Commons.

Many members around here have confidence in the Senate. I can understand that. They hope to go over there. But so far as handling these cases is concerned, I must say to him that confidence in Their Honours individually and respect for them though we may have, our confidence in their capacity to deal with divorce is shattered by what happened in respect of two cases which the hon. member for Parkdale says will be reported to the House of Commons with the preamble not proven. I have not read it in its entirety. I have read some of the sections having to do with the ladder story that my colleague the hon. member for Mackenzie reported to the committee. Incidentally I know that there was sworn evidence given by one person in that house that certain people were around there that night but without any ladder at all. My hon. friend reminds me that three different people swore that these people were around there without a ladder. Yet these people say they were

there with a ladder, which was a 2-foot ladder, up and down which three men were going.

speechtext:
The two-by-two game; yes. I suggest that the hon. member for York-Scarborough is defeating his own purpose. If he wants to boost the Senate and to boost our confidence in it, let him not relate it to this particular case. This case has all the earmarks of a ridiculous situation. If the committee is not prepared to do something else which others might be willing to do, I suggest that the least we should do is to agree that at some stage this Bill No. 434 should be referred back to the committee on miscellaneous private bills. I realize that the evidence in most of these fifty bills is contained in thin little pamphlets of only five, six or seven pages.
Not worth while reading it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I am referring to the ones that are before us. Their Honours have become so used to this routine that they can make a quick decision, but in this particular one the evidence runs to sixty-eight pages and apparently it went through our committee along with the other forty-nine without any consideration being given to it. 1 take it that although the case was contested in the other place the chairman of the miscellaneous private bills committee of this house did not advise the committee whether the people who contested it wished to continue that procedure before our committee.
But I think we have a responsibility, particularly now that doubts have been cast on the integrity of some of these detectives who have come here as witnesses, and now that doubts have been raised in our own minds as to the capacity of the senators to get to the heart of these cases. about this matter, it may soon be there again. If I do introduce it again I think I should give it a new subtitle. It might well be called "an act for the relief of parliament".

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the chairman of the committee or the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration-or both of them-a question, which I put forward in good faith. speechtext: When at five o'clock the house detoured into that unpleasant field of divorce I was dealing with the definition of the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
expression "totally and permanently disabled" and also with the definition of a similar term used in the Ontario act and in the Alberta act. It was indicated by me that Alberta, within the first year of the operation of its act to provide for pensions for certain disabled persons, encountered certain difficulties which made it necessary to amend their act within the period of twelve months.
The particular problem which confronted the government of Alberta in their act was in relation to those who may be mentally and physically disabled, but not so mentally disabled that they required hospitalization. I know that in the administration of their act it usually resulted in a decision that where mental and physical disability existed the deficiency was called "mental" and the person not pensionable.
We feel that when it comes to the definition of totally and permanently disabled persons probably the federal Department of National Health and Welfare, in consultation with the representatives of the provinces, will take that matter into consideration. It might seem that since Alberta has in its act defined disabled persons and also has a definition of chronic disability, we might urge that that definition of totally and permanently disabled persons be included in the bill which is before us at the present time; but we are not going to take that position. We believe that whatever definition is determined will result from negotiations between the federal department and the representatives of the respective departments of the provinces and that a properly negotiated definition of the term will emerge.
It may be that the same experience will be encountered that was encountered in my own province of Alberta within a period of a very few months after the act becomes law. It would then become necessary to amend the regulations or the act. We believe that if the definition is in the act it could not be amended without a statutory provision. If it were defined by regulation, then it is conceivable that it could be changed in the same way and rather quickly. For that reason we would prefer the definition to be established by regulation. However, we would say to the minister that if any change is to be made at any time after the first agreement is reached, such change should result only after proper negotiations with the provinces. We would hope that the federal Department of National Health and Welfare would not presume to take it upon itself arbitrarily to declare a change in the definition without consultation. We would not want that to happen under any circumstances. We feel that in every case there should be a truly negotiated change.
Disabled Persons-Allowances
I would add to that, certainly I do not consider myself qualified to define the expression "totally and permanently disabled". In this case, as I mentioned on other occasions, we must count upon those who have had some experience and who are in a better position to ascertain what might be a more generally acceptable definition. I think it goes without saying that whatever definition is determined would be applicable to all provinces; that there will not be any variation among the provinces.
It is to be noted that in Bill No. 462 the age of 18 is set as the qualifying age. It was indicated by the minister that that conforms with the Ontario act. My own province set the age at 21. I have not been so directed by the government of Alberta, nor have I any indication of what they intend doing, but I would hope-and I am also confident-that Alberta would see its way clear to accept the age of 18 as the qualifying age. After all, during the past year they have been assuming the full financial responsibility under their act which provides pensions for certain disabled persons. Now with the federal government assuming the responsibility of one-half of the cost, Alberta should be prepared to lower its age from 21 to 18. As I say, I hope and I am confident that they will do that, although I have no right to say so officially.
With respect to the proposed pension, we realize fully as a group here that one can argue that $40 is hopelessly inadequate to provide enough security for those people, but we are not going to press that at this time. We realize it is a new step. This legislation is being introduced and we assume it will be passed by parliament and will become law. That is the first step. But if we do not make an issue of $40 at this time, let it not be assumed or concluded that during the next session, or during subsequent sessions, we may not propose that it be increased.
The one thought that does go through my mind is this. Under the old age security and old age assistance acts the basic payment is $40 a month, and I presume the minister might to a degree anyway be justified in saying: We do not want this to be different from the payments under these acts. We realize fully of course that in many instances the earnings of the disabled will be nil, or at least considerably less than that of persons who qualify for old age assistance and old age security. However, that is a debatable question, if one bears in mind the fact that many of the older people, although they may be physically able to perform some work are not just acceptable generally to those who employ people. Therefore it is a highly debatable question. We see this bill as certainly

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Disabled Persons-Allowances a step in the right direction. Those people who have received nothing to date in the way of direct payments will receive $40 a month, and it will look like a fortune to many of them.
Let it not be assumed, as I said before, that if we do not labour that issue we feel it is a satisfactory amount, if one is looking on it as providing security. The minister will argue that it is not designed to provide security. We can see that argument, too.
The bill provides for a 10-year residential qualification. As a member of the old age security committee, I know we had to give very serious consideration to the matter of residence. We realized how easy it would be for people outside of our borders to suddenly rush into the country to qualify. For persons, let us say, in the United States, that would not be too difficult. They would not find too much difficulty in coming into our country. In this case they do not have to be subject to Canadian citizenship. Therefore we found it necessary to recommend that in the Old Age Assistance Act they had to reside in the country for 15 years and under the Old Age Security Act for 20 years. We have no particular objection to the provision that there should be a residence qualification. Even under the Alberta act they found it necessary to insert a residence qualification of 10 years because if a province had a provision to pay a pension to disabled persons and did not have a provision covering a residence qualification there would be an almost immediate influx of people from provinces all over the country. It became necessary, therefore, for the province of Alberta to have that residence qualification.
Earlier in this session, Mr. Speaker, in fact during the debate on the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) referred to the Alberta act and indicated-he did not use the word "discriminatory"-that with that provision it would have a bad effect upon unity in Canada. Of course he did say that it was maybe necessary to have that provision. Well, I feel it certainly was necessary to have it, and it is just as necessary in an act of this kind to have residential qualifications. There may be a situation developed in Canada where one or more provinces may take advantage of this act. Then, of course, you would have the position of the 10 years' residential qualification running into a rather unusual situation where a person may move from one province, where they pay no disability pension, to another province where they do make that payment. I do not know what would happen under that situation because they might well have been residents in Canada for the 10-year period.

Probably this was discussed when the minister held a conference with the representatives of the province. All these matters are important. As the bill progresses through its various stages we may well have questions to ask on such matters.
In his early remarks the minister indicated that the situation as it existed with regard to disabled persons constitutes a real burden upon their relatives and friends. Well, most of us know that, and I certainly know from my own personal experience in view of the cases with which I have had to deal. It is a real tragedy for many people. In fact, I know of one couple who have reached the old age security stage and they have a daughter who is approximately 30 years of age. She is unable to provide for herself and her parents want to keep her at home. Her condition is a combination of mental and physical and they feel she is their responsibility. But they have to live upon old age security payments and it is quite a struggle for them. Of course what disturbs them more than anything else is what will happen to their dependent when they pass away.
In this bill we have at least provided a partial answer to that problem. In another particular case I think I found one of the most tragic experiences I have ever had as a member of parliament. This concerned a man who was 60 years of age who came to me for advice. He had resided within this country for a period of 40 years and he had been successful as a farmer but he developed arthritis and over a period of years it had taken practically everything he had been able to acquire in order to try and secure some relief for his disability. He, like so many other people, followed up every suggestion good or bad in order to find relief until in the end he was without means. His wife was compelled to scrub floors in order that the two of them might be able to get along. He communicated with me and he did not fit in anywhere. I thought it was a terrible tragedy for me as a representative of this country and a member of parliament in this great nation to have to tell him that his only hope was municipal relief. I cannot recall anything which hurt me more than that particular case.
This is the type of case which will be covered under the bill which is now before us and one need not go beyond that particular case to appreciate the value of the general principle contained in this bill.
The minister said, though he may not have used these exact words, that we would share the burdens these people have to bear. I agree with that absolutely. Certainly those

of us who are more fortunate from a physical point of view have no cause to complain about sharing the burden which these people have had visited upon them through no choice of their own, and for any nation like this to be able to fill that gap is certainly a step forward.
In the early course of my observations I may have been somewhat critical. In fact, the minister by his interjection has remarked to that effect. I was critical but he will appreciate that we see in this bill a real step forward and something which we have no hesitation in supporting at all in principle, and if I know this House of Commons, as I have known other houses in the past, then I would suggest that there will be few and probably no dissenting voices in this parliament. But once again, however, I do not want a statement of that kind to be construed as meaning that we accept it in every detail.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it would be the easiest thing in the world to go on discussing this measure and occupy the entire 40 minutes at my disposal. But I do not intend to do that. To the extent that I have already spoken I have probably held up the passage of this measure. If that be true then possibly I should apologize. We in this group certainly support the bill before the house at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I know I have no more right to speak on this bill than any other hon. member in this house, but I have some right and I wish now to express my gratitude to the minister for introducing this measure. When I came here in 1935 this was one of the things about which I spoke. I have continued to do so every year since because I felt then as I have felt ever since that those who could not earn a dollar were forgotten people, but that they were not forgotten people after that.
I am not going to speak very long tonight because I have spoken loud and long in the past on this subject and I must say that I received first class support from all around me, especially after the session was over when the minister supported me in my views. I am not forgotting the former minister of national health and welfare, the late Senator Ian Mackenzie. When I had spoken on this matter on about the fourth occasion he said: "Dan, stick to it. You are right."
The Christian program is, feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and help those who cannot help themselves. Very plain and simple. But, of course, we sometimes feel the government should do more and we are not always willing to put our hand in our own pocket and help those who
Disabled Persons-Allowances cannot help themselves. But personally I think hon. members of this house even in that way take second place to no other group of men in Canada.
I admit I received considerable support from the trades and labour council of Fort William, and Jim Walsh, who was then president, gave me a complete list of disabled persons. I was alarmed because I did not realize there were so many but of course the trades and labour council were in possession of that information because they were always interested.
I paid my tribute three years ago to the present Minister of Labour, the V.C. on this side of the house who has a good heart in him too, and who gave me any information he had on the subject. He told me that his department and the Department of Veterans Affairs and the department of national health were co-operating with the provinces all over Canada in trying to help disabled persons.
Two years ago, before the election, when we debated this question in a full and complete manner, I will not forget, and I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will not forget either, that I thanked the minister when he promised consideration for this problem. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said I had more confidence in the minister than he had. If he looks up Hansard he will find that. Indeed, the hon. member has now agreed with me and while my first name is the name of a prophet I think my prognostication was a little more accurate than his at that time. A little more than a year ago I commended the province of Ontario for leading the band. No matter what party is in power we expect the province of Ontario to lead the way because we are the crack province of Canada. They led the way in bringing in this pension for disabled persons.
Mr. Speaker, I have been in the homes of some of those disabled persons who have received the pension. May I say that it would do anyone's heart good to hear them express their gratitude for the $40 a month. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) says that it is not enough. May I say too with him that $40 more than nothing is a great deal of money to people who previously had not had a dollar of their own. Just to feel that stiff cheque in his hand for the first time gives such a person a great thrill.
I know there will be difficulties in administering this bill. As to the definition, I would be well satisfied to take the definition upon which the province of Ontario grants their pension. It will be fairly close to what is right. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that the federal government

Disabled Persons-Allowances should pay 75 per cent of the cost and the province should pay 25 per cent. I do not see much sense in that proposition. I speak for the province of Ontario now. If the province of Ontario is paying the whole thing, why should we discredit the province of Ontario by offering them 75 per cent of the whole 100 per cent they are now paying? Why should we offer the 75-25 per cent basis to a province like Alberta? I was going to say that that is a province which has more money than it knows how to handle, but I will not say that. Would we offer the basis of 75-25 per cent to British Columbia? Would we offer the basis of 75-25 per cent to Quebec? They would tell you, "We will pay for our own pension". It may be that there are some provinces which will find difficulty in this matter. I am sure that the dominion government will not be lacking in their willingness to co-operate.
The only thing I want to say is this: While there are those in the opposition who have tried to pull this bill to pieces and- they did not say it was almost bad but they would not say it was almost good-to show the weaknesses of the bill, but I just take this opportunity, in my own humble way, of thanking the minister for his co-operation. He never gave me anything else. Three years ago we let the resolution go by and did not debate it. He said: You will get co-operation just as soon as the government is ready. Now the minister does not take credit for this bill; he gives the government credit. He knows that he is not the government. However, he is an extremely important part of it as far as this bill is concerned.
I am not afraid of what the future may hold for this bill. There may be considerable difficulty, but it will be a great help to those who have not had a dollar coming in. I have had letters from all over Canada, from Cape Breton to Victoria. One little girl wrote me from Cape Breton the other day to this effect: We hope it will come; I have never earned a dollar and unless Providence does something for me, I never shall earn a dollar. To any cabinet minister or any member of this house who can be a partner in giving a girl like that a pension it must give a feeling of happiness to be alive and to be a member of this house.
I just conclude by saying "Thank you, Mr. Minister; may you keep on going because in every department in which you have worked or which you have headed up you have done something that made Canada sit up and take notice". Just think of it. As to those of us who were not born in Canada but who were born some place else and are still living here, whether we were Scots, Irish, English, Italian,


Russian or something else, we are not that any more. I am not an Irishman any more; I am a Canadian. I was born in the land that I left in order to choose what I thought was a better country to come to, and I am loyal to my native land. I just thank the minister and say this to him: Keep on and may Providence be with you.

Mr. Speaker, since I am one of those who have been requesting for the past few years in the house the enactment of legislation to provide help for our disabled citizens, I feel justified in participating in the present debate, even if I speak for only two or three minutes.
May I first congratulate the government on this truly social legislation. If I were one of those whose duty it is to criticize I would say that it comes a little late, but I believe I can disregard that fact and congratulate the government for finally agreeing to introduce this social legislation.
However, I must qualify my statement by making a suggestion to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) through you, Mr. Speaker. In my humble opinion, the age at which the disabled person will be entitled to receive a pension-provided the other conditions have been satisfactorily met-is a little too high, since in certain cases, at the age of 18, the anatomic lesion or functional trouble has become permanent and cannot be cured no matter what treatment is applied at that time.
Therefore, we should get the assurance that rehabilitation treatments will be given in due time, when they have the most chances of succeeding. I know that the lowering of the age of eligibility to 15, to 10, and even to the time of birth, would greatly upset the provisions of the bill now before us.
However, if it were impossible to lower the age limit provided in the bill in an absolute way, I would be tempted to make to the government, in order to remedy this situation, the following suggestion: in my opinion, this bill should provide for payments from the time of birth in certain cases, or later, in the specific cases where these children or these young people undergo medical treatment for rehabilitation, and this as long as the invalidity lasted and treatments were given. In addition to the moral support to which I referred a moment ago and which I shall not discuss further, this procedure would facilitate rehabilitation, which, I can well imagine, is the ultimate dream of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

In any event, this suggestion would bring about savings of public funds since a relatively large number of these people who would have undergone treatment from an early age would have become normal men or women who would no longer fall within the category of those assisted by the bill under consideration at this time. And what is more important still, a number of them would have become quite normal by the time they would be coming into contact with society. They would therefore have a far better chance of normal rehabilitation.
When I say that by promoting the early rehabilitation of a large number of these invalids, the government would save money, I will not be contradicted, I am sure, by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. If I have understood his remarks properly, this afternoon, he mentioned that a number of veterans, for instance, have been put in a position where they are now once more able to lead a fairly normal life after undergoing rehabilitation. As a matter of fact, the same is true of assisted and rehabilitated blind people.
It is, in fact, that part of the minister's remarks, added to my modest medical knowledge, which have prompted me to say the few words I have just said and which I now immediately bring to a close, submitting them most sincerely to the attention of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I expected this to be a very happy day because it seemed to me that all parties in the house would hail with real satisfaction the introduction of this bill which marks such a great forward step in the setting up of the welfare state in Canada. However, I was astonished to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I think that never before in my life, and I admit I am getting on in years now, have I heard an hon. gentleman find so much cause for gloom in something that is so obviously good. I should have thought that of all the political parties in the house that hail the bill with satisfaction the hon. members who sit opposite me would have hailed it with the most satisfaction, knowing as they do that the Liberals have some common ground with them on the question of social welfare and differ from them only with respect to that kind of socialism that has to do with the social ownership of certain public utilities.
I should have thought they would have been overjoyed at the fact that the Liberals
Disabled Persons-Allowances had introduced this new and large measure of the welfare state in Canada. But what do we find? We find that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre sees nothing but cause for unmitigated gloom in the bill that has been introduced in the house today.

So far as some of the speeches the hon. member has made are concerned, I have agreed entirely and I have not hesitated to vote with him even against the majority on this side of the house when I thought he had said something sensible. But when he talks such sheer unmitigated poppycock as he talks today then I find that I cannot go along with him. I must say that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre reminds me of a certain character in "Pilgrim's Progress". We have so many exclergymen in the house that maybe they will be able to remind me of which one it is, but it is a character in "Pilgrim's Progress" who, no matter how good things were, always found something wrong with them. I think if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre went to a wonderful wedding and got a great big slice of wedding cake he would go home and complain that he hurt a tooth on a pebble in one corner of the cake. I am very much afraid that on the day after he gets past St. Peter and is admitted within the pearly gates he will be complaining that although the streets are paved with gold there should also be diamonds in the gold-paved streets. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I think that every intelligent person-
That counts you out.

-in the Dominion of Canada will know perfectly well that what we have done today is to pass a great milestone in the social welfare set-up of the Dominion of Canada. I think if we have any great weakness it is perhaps partly due to the hon. gentlemen opposite who are such experts at
5354	HOUSE OF
Disabled Persons-Allowances crying blue ruin even about the social welfare advances that we do make. However, in my opinion every intelligent citizen in Canada will know perfectly well that we have passed a great milestone in our social welfare system. I think that the Canadian people have some weaknesses and one of them is that we do not think highly enough of our own achievements.
One of the great advantages of travelling in all the different countries of the world is that you find out that, regardless of the political persuasion of the people you meet, Canada's prestige stands high with all the nations of the world. You will find that while you may get an argument about some things you will not get an argument about the statement that Canada has the finest welfare state system of any country in the western hemisphere and is even miles ahead of our great and rich neighbour to the south, the United States. As an example of that I have in my hand a copy of The Reporter, a very reputable magazine published in the United States. It is the issue of April 27, 1954 and it contains an article by state senator Richard L. Neuberger of Portland, Oregon, on Canada's social security system for children. He gives the origin of our welfare state system in Canada dating it from the report of Professor Leonard Marsh of my own home town of Vancouver. He has this to say:
The last time millions of Americans were out of work their craving for assurance against want produced unemployment compensation, old age assistance, and our entire system of social security benefits. If such economic hardships occur again, a new phrase is likely to be heard in the land: "family allowances."
Then he goes on at great length to show how family allowances, the great reform enacted by the Liberal government headed by the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, have been such a great advantage to this country, how we have set the pace for all the other countries of the western hemisphere and how far ahead of those countries we are.
I want to touch briefly on an extremely important point made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) with respect to the health grants of 1948. I think that the people of Canada have not yet realized how tremendously important those health grants are. I happen to have had experience of that from the receiving end because not so much by my own decision but more or less because pressure was put on me to take the job I became the first British Columbia president of the Canadian Arthritis and Rheumatism Society, a society which achieved a marvellous expansion right across the country. Whereas it started in


the first instance only a few years ago with no facilities, no technicians and no treatment facilities we all know that now the facilities stretch pretty well across the country.
British Columbia has set an example for the whole of Canada. We set out only a few years ago without a single dollar of funds but with the realization of a great need. We happened to have in that province a very fine woman who was the sparkplug of the whole thing. She more or less stampeded me into the job. I must say that we had great co-operation from the Department of National Health and Welfare from the very beginning. When we first started out we were almost embarrassed by the amount of help we got from the department in the way of actual facilities. That great work would never have been able to spread across the country in the way it has if that help had not been available from the very beginning to give us the physical equipment needed to carry out that particular job. As I say, if you go right down the list I think hon. members know perfectly well, I suppose, that everyone in this house, or for that matter and out of it, says silly things at times or things that we do not mean seriously-
Hear, hear.
-and I will be the first to admit that I have done my share. But let us never forget this. Whatever else we fight about, let us not belittle the great social welfare-
Take your own advice.

-system which we have set up in this Dominion of Canada. We have a very fine system here, of which every patriotic Canadian should well be proud.
I know quite well that this bill is not perfect. I know quite well that the social welfare system of Canada is not perfect. I am reminded of the time when the great evangelist Dwight L. Moodie remarked during one of his sermons that he had never met any perfect people. After the sermon one of the congregation came up to complain. He said that he was a perfect man, whereupon Mr. Moodie remarked "are you married?" The gentleman said, "yes". He said, "I should like to have a word with your wife". Now, there may be completely perfect people in the group opposite; there may be completely perfect social welfare measures in the group opposite. However, I feel we have not done too badly in our social welfare state system in this Dominion of Canada. I, for one, am glad to see that so far as we can possibly discover up to now there is no one in this house who is willing to stand up and say he is opposed to this system.

The great advance in our time was when family allowances were introduced into Canada. As we all know, a prominent leader, whose name I shall not mention at this time, took a very prominent position contrary to family allowances. In this analysis written by state senator Richard Neuberger, in the magazine The Reporter, he attributes one of the successes of the Liberal party over many years, and one of the causes of the nonsuccess of a certain other party that I shall not name now, to the fact that in the early days they took such a strong position on family allowances. I, for one, have never been the slightest bit taken aback by the gibes we hear from some hon. members opposite concerning silk-hatted socialists. I have never been taken aback when we were accused of setting up a welfare state. Now, I find even some Conservatives in some other countries are not the slightest bit backward about taking responsibility for setting up the welfare state.
I had the great privilege during the last general election campaign in Great Britain of being sent over in a professional capacity to write about the political campaigns. I heard six of the seven speeches made by that great leader of the Conservative party, the then Right Hon. Mr. Winston Churchill. I may say it was a wonderful experience for me to hear that grand old war horse, and to see him winning an election by making only seven speeches. Six of those speeches were just a half hour long, and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, I intend to follow his example and stay within my half hour. I shall never forget being at his nomination meeting, which they call an adoption meeting, and he was anwering questions from the floor. Someone asked him, "Is it true that the Labourites inaugurated the welfare state?" The grand old Conservative gentleman rose and said, "The welfare state, I invented it". That is the leader of the Conservative party speaking. Then he went on to give the reasons for saying that it was under his government, during wartime, that he laid the foundation for the welfare state.
However we may argue about small things that do not matter-
Hear, hear.

-let us not belittle the really great social advances that we are making. Let the hon. gentlemen opposite who find it so difficult to give credit where credit is due acknowledge at least that the Liberal government has made a great forward step in this system of the welfare state. The other day the young Liberals of Canada presented to the great Prime Minister of this country, and the leader of this Liberal party, a very fine
Disabled Persons-Allowances bronze bust. The real memorial to the Prime Minister of this country will not be found in anything made of bronze, but it will be found in the regard of the people of Canada for the great statesman who set up the great system and made the great forward step in the welfare state, which keeps this Canada ahead of the whole western hemisphere.

The
remarks of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), Mr. Speaker, cannot have failed to add to the self-satisfaction already so adequately expressed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) on his own account. In support of, and as a basis for, this self-satisfaction the minister told at some considerable length of the work that had been done and the results that had been achieved by other people. It is true that he did mention some few grants the government had given to these organizations, but he carefully refrained from speaking of the percentage those grants represented of the total that had been expended on these projects.
The proposal embodied in this bill is meritorious. I do not believe any hon. member could have serious objection to the principle involved. If we are going to pay pensions to individuals solely because they have reached the age of 70 years, irrespective of their earning capacity, then the payment of pensions to those permanently barred from earning a livelihood either through injury or disease should logically apply with even greater force. However, there is a consideration applicable to this latter group of which the bill as drafted takes no cognizance. It is important, of course, to see that the totally disabled person possesses sufficient financial resources to provide the ordinary necessities of life, food, clothing and shelter. But it is of even greater importance to retrain the individual to live within the limits of his possibilities and to the hilt of his capabilities.
I cannot believe that the. minister is so indifferent to the opportunities presented to him at this time as to ignore the prospect of establishing modern facilities throughout the country for the retraining and rehabilitation of the totally disabled. What sort of answer to the pitiful plea of the supposedly hopeless cripple is it to say, "We will provide you with a pittance sufficient to enable you to live in your misery for the period of your life expectancy, but we can offer you no hope of an improvement in your condition." This attitude might be justified, if there was really no hope of re-establishing those seemingly hopeless cripples.

The hon. member has asked me a question. I certainly spent a good deal of time pointing out what we were prepared to do in the field of rehabilitation, which is associated with this measure.
I wish the minister would indicate to what extent, and how much money.
I did. I guess my hon. friend was not in the house at the time, or he would not be saying this.

This, however, is by no means the case, as the minister is no doubt aware. Several agencies in this country and in the United States are doing excellent work in this connection. Among those that might be mentioned is the Ontario compensation board at Malton, which is achieving remarkable results in the rehabilitation of victims of industrial accidents.
We heard all that from the minister today.

But it is not the minister's department that is doing it, you will notice. The Department of Veterans Affairs, which incidentally happens to be a department of government-and I will give them full credit for this-is engaged in the treatment and retraining of paraplegics at several centres. They could do a lot more. Perhaps the best known work of this nature on this continent is being carried out at New York University, Bellevue Medical Centre, at the Institute of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation.
Dr. Howard A. Rusk of New York city, reporting in the Journal of the American Medical Association in the issue of November 1, 1952, surveys the results achieved in 208 cases discharged from this institution, taken consecutively. This report emphasizes the really remarkable results that can be achieved by a comprehensive program of retraining among a group of helpless and hopeless cripples. For instance, 97 per cent received some benefit from their rehabilitation experience. The number confined to wheelchairs and beds decreased from 67-8 per cent to 32-2 per cent of the total, and the number of bedfast included, decreased from 36-1 per cent to 11-1 per cent. The number able to do some kind of work increased from 18-3 per cent to 59-6 per cent, and the number incapable of even minimum self-care decreased from 63 per cent to 18-3 per cent. This latter figure is a true index of the economic value of the program.
From the point of view of direct measurable gain in dollars and cents-the cost of rehabilitating 49 of the patients to a stage


where they were able to engage in gainful employment was $140,000 and the annual earnings of this same group after rehabilitation totalled $94,000-not a bad return on investment. From the point of view of overall significance to the community of this type of program, I quote the conclusions of Dr. Rusk in the article referred to:
1. Rehabilitation pays dividends in dollars as well as in social returns. 2. Rehabilitation of severely disabled persons who may be potentially unemployable is no less valuable economically than rehabilitation of the less severely disabled who are potentially employable. 3. There is need for improvement and expansion of the administrative types of social service focused on development and use of resources in the environment. The hopeful finding of this study is that, with physical rehabilitation and adequate social support, the disabled person can "learn to live and work with what he has left".
Surely the government can require no more convincing evidence of the value of an organized program of rehabilitation for the disabled, both from the viewpoint of straight economic return on this investment, and from the aspect of freeing this hitherto neglected group of citizens from the shackles of enforced immobility.
I would suggest that the minister should enter into discussions with the provinces with the object of establishing at least one completely equipped and staffed institute of physical medicine and rehabilitation in each province, the cost to be distributed according to the respective financial capabilities of provincial and federal governments respectively.
In support of my contention that pensions alone are no solution to the problems of the totally disabled, may I quote a personal communication from Dr. Leona Baumgartner, commissioner of health of New York city, who has had a wealth of experience with this subject and who states:
In regard to the question about the relative advantage of allocation of funds for rehabilitation purposes, rather than pensions and custodial facilities, there is no question that diagnostic treatment and rehabilitation services when carried on by well trained personnel can do much to change the outlook and potentiality of some custodial or public assistance patients to the point of helping them become independent, useful, self-supporting and productive members of society. It is undoubtedly true that such intensive measures will not be equally effective for all patients. However, until our scientific knowledge develops more, some custodial facilities and pensions will still be required, but perhaps less so than are now used as more and better rehabilitation services are developed.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the minister may plead that this is a provincial responsibility, which is undoubtedly true, but the minister

has in the past shown himself as not without aptitude in circumventing such constitutional restrictions. Let him make use of his old device of matching grants in aid.
Mr. Speaker, there is no question of the existence of this problem in Canada, and likewise no question of the inadequacy of present machinery to deal with it effectively. In my opinion, the minister would be recreant to his responsibilities did he not seize the opportunity presented by this proposed legislation to see to it that a really comprehensive program of rehabilitation is made available on a nation-wide basis for our totally disabled citizens. It would be a simple matter to make suitable provision to this end in the proposed legislation. The minister indicates that he has already made it in other legislation, with which I am not familiar. I hope that that is a fact. The challenge is to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Will he meet it?
If I thought there was any virtue in repetition and reiteration, I would probably weary the house with appeals to the government and the minister to widen the scope of this legislation in order to provide Canada with thoroughly modern, comprehensive rehabilitation facilities.
A rapidly increasing accumulation of experience in the United States proves that rehabilitation is economically feasible, but equally important that it is an economic necessity, and it gets worse and worse as our population gets older and older. The federal government of the United States recognizes this fact and gives active financial support to state and municipal governments towards the provision of facilities. Contrast this enlightened recognition of reality with the meagre, almost infinitesimal assistance provided to the provinces and municipalities by our federal government.
In case any hon. member is not impressed by the very substantial economic value to the nation of the program which I am advocating, I would like to put on the record some figures from the American experience which I would hope might impress the minister, and which I am certain are bound to impress his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I shall do this by quoting from an article entitled "The Economic Values of Rehabilitation" by McCoy, Rusk and Koch in the January 1954 number of the New York State Journal of Medicine:
To sharpen our focus on these values, let us examine the figures for the year 1952. The 88 state divisions of vocational rehabilitation and agencies for the blind in that year gave some kind of rehabilitation service to more than 228,000 disabled individuals. In the same period they rehabilitated successfully 63,632 men and women. The entire

cost of operation of the state-federal program was about $32 million. It is estimated that the annual earnings of the 63,632 men and women successfully rehabilitated will be in excess of $115,420,000. It is further estimated that in the first year after their rehabilitation they will pay in federal income tax from their earnings approximately $10,378,000 and that during their remaining working life they will pay about $270 million in federal income taxes! At this rate we are receiving from the successfully rehabilitated people $12 in federal income tax for each $1 of federal money spent.
In the light of evidence such as this I submit that the question is not whether or not Canada can afford a program of rehabilitation, but rather whether Canada can afford not to embark on such a program.

With respect to the matter of bringing politics into this debate, the minister did that very early in the game. My hon. friend, the member for Vancouver South, referred to Sir Winston Churchill. I am reminded of an observation made by another great Churchill, Sir Winston's father.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that what I shall have to say will to some extent pour oil on troubled waters, and having had an experience once today I shall be very careful that I say nothing which can be misinterpreted. Something has been said in criticism of the minister for taking unto this government, to himself, and some hon. members on this side of the house, a certain amount of credit for introducing the bill now under discussion. I think it is true to say that at the same time the minister did give credit to other hon. members situated in other parts of the house. No one would ever contend that the measures we introduce do not sometimes have their inspiration from hon. members on the opposite side of the house. In fact, it would be a tragedy if that were not so.
Still, Mr. Speaker, I do rise with a good deal of satisfaction to support the measure which is going to provide allowances for disabled persons. This measure, completing, as I think it does, a broad pattern of social legislation, is one which all hon. members of this house, and indeed all the people of Canada whom we represent, will approve and applaud. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is to be congratulated I think, as the responsible minister of this government, on the completion of the over-all plan. It must give him and his officials great satisfaction to realize that all classes of our people who have a legitimate claim upon the heart and purse of this country are now taken care of.
It is not without value to note that this government, chiefly through this department and the Department of Veterans Affairs, provides for assistance to the young through family allowances, and the old through old age security and old age assistance, leaving the middle group, the young and the vigorous, to fend for themselves and, in addition, to help bear the burdens of those in other groups.
Disabled Persons-Allowances
The blind and the war veterans, being special groups, are treated as such, leaving only those who suffer a disability not attributable either to blindness, war service, or industrial accident. It is well to note the similarity in the measure of assistance to be given. For the most part, the allowances are the same in amount, and all require some form of means test. In my opinion, this is as it should be. Note also that allowances are to be paid for total and permanent disability. Herein lies the chief difficulty. Mention has already been made by other speakers of this problem and I will not develop it further, as I intended to do, because I have confidence in the skill and sympathetic attitude of the minister and his very competent officials to arrive at a satisfactory and reasonable interpretation of what this parliament means by "permanent disability".
Here, Mr. Speaker, I leave the field of administration and finance to venture into the field of the theory of social welfare. Is this a good measure? What is the chief aim of measures of this kind? Is it to rid ourselves of the uncomfortable feeling that others of our people suffer, chiefly through no fault of their own? Do we achieve this by the payment of a sum of money which will assist them to exist?
I have sufficient knowledge and faith in the sense of responsibility of our people and this parliament to reject this as a complete answer, and to make the claim that our ultimate aim is to build up the physical and emotional state of each of these unfortunate people so that they can become able and willing contributors to the society of which they are members.
It would be wrong simply to pension people off. All the measures sponsored by this government in this field are measures of assistance. None are intended to be more than that. To deprive a person of the incentive to strive for himself is morally wrong and does not achieve the purpose which is set before us. For one thing, the amount of assistance is never enough. The more nearly the amount of assistance is to a subsistence level the more dependent does the recipient become and the less likely is he or she to put forth that effort which contributes to healthful living.
While I approve, Mr. Speaker, a reasonable and even a generous measure of assistance tc those who cannot under any circumstances fend for themselves, I do emphasize the wisdom of keeping ever before us the possibility of rehabilitation. There are degrees of disability. No person is without some form of disability and, indeed, there are some
