For this reason, Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that this act should be considered in relation to an act we passed a few days ago called the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act. When I spoke to the committee concerning the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act on March 3 of this year I stated that in my opinion it was one of the most forwardlooking pieces of legislation to come before the house at this session. I did so because the only really important section of that amending act was the introduction of the idea of a training program for the physically handicapped. It is to be known as schedule R. This too is a measure to be undertaken in co-operation with the provinces.
I would remind hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that training for physically disabled persons has been going on for about four years under a scheme sponsored by the Department of Labour with the blessing of the Department of National Health and Welfare. During this time under a different schedule-schedule M it was called-approximately 500 persons suffering various disabilities have been trained and have been found suitable and adequate employment. I am informed that over 80 per cent of those trained in that special group are satisfactorily rehabilitated.
From this small sampling our minds turn to the possibilities in a scheme of this kind. Not only will the public purse be saved tremendous sums which would otherwise be spent without apparent results, but there is reason to hope that thousands of our citizens can, by a combination of these two measures, be restored to participation and partnership in the business of developing this great country of ours.
This is a measure, Mr. Speaker, which I am sure-because it appeals to the best in our nature-will meet with approval in all

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a brief contribution to the discussion this evening largely arising out of certain remarks that have been made during the past hour or so. I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) made an excellent contribution to the debate this evening in helping to bring it back into focus again. It more or less got off the track to a certain extent following the contribution of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott).
In listening to various comments earlier in the discussion with respect to the introduction of disability pensions for the totally disabled, it seemed to me that there was general approval on all sides of the house. The sentiment was also expressed in all quarters of the house that the measure was long overdue. Since I became a member of the House of Commons one of the social welfare topics that has been discussed most frequently in various debates has been the pressing need to consider the special problem of our totally and permanently disabled citizens. At the time these discussions took place I wondered why the federal government had not taken action earlier.
As has already been indicated, this area has been pioneered by municipalities, provincial governments and voluntary groups such as the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. So far as I can see, what is happening now with the introduction of this measure is that the federal government is at long last acknowledging some financial responsibility. This is only as it should be. We know that the central government has tended to reserve to itself the more lucrative tax fields. Such being the case, it is only right that the dominion government should at this time accept some financial responsibility and come to the aid of the municipalities, the provincial governments and the voluntary groups who have had to cope with the challenge of this special social welfare problem. Somebody has been looking after these people. It goes without saying that the totally disabled have not been neglected completely. I know from personal experience that where no other
5362	HOUSE OF
Disabled Persons-Allowances means of financial support have been available it has fallen upon municipal governments to provide from their inadequate tax resources a bare minimum of existence for these unfortunate people.
As the result of federal action in co-operation with the provincial governments the whole matter will now be co-ordinated and placed on a much sounder basis. I was interested in the interpretation that the hon. member for Vancouver South placed upon this measure. He regarded it as another milestone along the road to the welfare state. I am inclined to suggest that his social philosophy is somewhat out of date because, while it is true that during the early thirties it was accepted somewhat uncritically that the state should meet basic welfare needs, in more recent years there has been a considerable change in that viewpoint. Serious thinkers in the field have now come to the conclusion that the state cannot meet the demands of social welfare.
The state is a cold, remote governing body that certainly cannot get down to the intimate levels necessary to provide in the nation an adequate atmosphere of social welfare and social security. Therefore I do not regard the measure as another step forward to the mythical social welfare state. I regard it as merely a common-sense approach to a problem that has been with us from time immemorial, a problem that those with inadequate financial resources have attempted to cope with as best they could. All that the federal government is doing is opening its bountiful treasury and providing some financial assistance to meet a situation of real distress.
As 1 see it, that is all that the federal government can do with respect to meeting the demands of social welfare in the country. In the final analysis social welfare is the concern of the basic social institutions. The government is helpless if the family, the school and the church are not performing their functions. It is on that level that the real social needs are met, and modern social science is recognizing that principle. If this legislation is going to achieve the desired result in meeting the pressing demands of the totally disabled in an adequate way, it will depend upon the co-operation of the families.
The families still have responsibilities for the totally disabled. True enough, they will receive some financial assistance. As has been pointed out by every speaker, it would also depend upon the full co-operation of our technical schools, our vocational training schools, who are moving forward to embrace more adequate vocational rehabilitation programs. As has been pointed out, if we


are going to really meet the situation the two must go hand in hand, the financial provision must work very closely with adequate rehabilitation services.
Every rehabilitation case has to be measured on its own merits, has to be thoroughly evaluated by rehabilitation counsellors. If you try the shotgun approach to the problem and spread certain moneys over a large area without any attempt to meet the individual need then, of course, the second state is worse than the first. If we are really going to meet the basic social welfare need, it will depend upon successful operation and functioning of these basic social institutions. Included in the group, of course, are the local community groups or neighbourhood groups. No one can feel he is surrounded by an atmosphere of social security unless he is living in a situation that provides this intimate person-to-person relationship, and that cannot be provided from a remote set-up but by the intimate, warm and personal contact of your local neighbourhood groups.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that this measure will assist to a considerable extent in making it possible for these basic social institutions, these local groups, to deal with the problem with which they have already been trying to cope-with inadequate financial resources. Now that they have this assistance we should see a real improvement in meeting this problem.

In rising to support this bill, Mr. Speaker, I want to pay tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who late last summer announced a decision to help these unfortunate Canadians who are totally and permanently disabled. This decision on the part of the Prime Minister indicates to me his great humanitarianism. I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) for bringing forward this legislation at this time. In spite of what the opposition has said about the bill he should get a great deal of satisfaction from bringing forward this further measure of social security. The fact remains that no matter who tries to take credit for this bill, he introduced it.
I may say that I have had many representations from the totally and permanently disabled. I have seen a number of them in my practice. It is sad to see these people dependent on other people for a livelihood. From now on they will get some help, will have some income and will not be so dependent upon relatives, agencies or people in the neighbourhood. Many of us heard an excellent lecture a week ago on anterior poliomyelitis, commonly known as infantile paralysis,

as one of the causes of permanent disability. It is not as frequent as some other causes. In fact the total number of cases of permanent disability is a very small percentage of the total number of cases. It is true that many have residual paralysis, and they may have it for a long time or may have it for a lifetime. They get some relief through improvement and some relief from mechanical means.
The minister, I believe, mentioned some of the diseases causing permanent and total disability. He mentioned disseminated sclerosis, progressive muscular atrophy, rheumatoid arthritis. We have also different congenital anomalies and one very common cause of which we are getting a number of cases in recent years is the result of highway accidents. Many victims receive severe brain and spinal cord injuries that are irreparable. We think it is up to the provinces to cut down accidents on the highways, and some of the provinces are doing a great deal in this respect. Many of these people are in hospitals for months, even years. Some of them are an expense to the municipalities and the provinces concerned.
These pensions are being awarded on a matching basis between the federal government and the provinces. I feel it is well that is so because the question of permanent disability is linked with rehabilitation, which is a joint responsibility of the federal and provincial governments. I agree with the minister and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) that it will be difficult to get a proper definition for permanent and total disability. With the modem advances in therapy and in rehabilitation, a person who ten years ago might have been considered totally and permanently disabled might not be considered so today. I would hope that in the interpretation of this act generous consideration will be given so that all deserving cases will get a pension.

I had not
intended to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, but as a British Columbian I feel I have to do so after having listened to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). I have observed with considerable interest, in fact great interest, ever since I came here last November, the unrelieved relish that the hon. member displays for the taste of the polish on the shoes of the Liberal ministry. But today, I think he exceeded himself. If the Minister of
National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin)______
I was going to say displayed but of course that would not be displaying-had even simulated a certain modest diffidence, none of this would have occurred. Naturally, when he strides before the house as the harbinger 83276-3391
Disabled Persons-Allowances of all good things to the people of Canada, when he takes all the credit for this very mediocre piece of legislation, when he denies credit to those who were advocating it while he was opposing it, then naturally he is going to get a kick-back. Naturally, those who feel that this is a great piece of unfairness are going to be rather savage in their return.
Then, of course, that brings us to the position of that great champion of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Vancouver South. I am not going to recite, as I could do, all the various turns and changes of this political chameleon. I remember, however, an occasion when in his column he defended the election of a very well known communist in British Columbia, the leader of the Labour-Progressive party, Nigel Morgan. The hon. member in his column advocated that this gentleman should be elected to the legislature.
I also recall that there was a time when he was going to be barred from the radio because of his subversive utterances. And who was it who came to his rescue? Well, curiously enough-and most misguidedly now, it appears-it was the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) who insisted that the hon. gentleman who is now the representative in this House of Commons for Vancouver South should be accorded freedom of speech, and even after today I am sure that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and all those who sit with him, would still demand that the hon. member for Vancouver South should have complete freedom of speech-even though he uses that freedom in such a strange way.
But look what he does for us.

Yes, definitely, he does a lot for us. But when we are told that we should greet today as a day of great joy because, after incessant prodding by people outside the Liberal party, and after incessant prodding from organizations all over Canada, the government finally and reluctantly brings in a most inadequate measure to deal with the present social problem; I say that when the hon. member for Vancouver South suggests that we should greet this even with loud hosannas in this day and age, then I begin to wonder about this freedom of speech, and whether it should not be coupled with a certain measure of intelligence. I have heard the hon. gentleman reach a number of milestones on the way to the new Jerusalem since I came here to the House of Commons. Sometimes I think it is another

Disabled Persons-Allowances kind of milestone, one we are told in the Scriptures which paved the road to other places.
' This measure has been introduced, and the : party to which I belong is prepared to support it. However it is not prepared to turn handsprings of delight. It is not prepared to pretend that this is an adequate measure. It is not prepared to pretend that it is an indication of public-spiritedness on the part of the government; because it is very obvious that all that has happened here today is what has happened time and again since this very party assumed power in Canada; when pressure becomes irresistible, then finally they move. When they move they demand tremendous credit and accolades for having moved in the face of irresistible pressure. I suppose we are always going to have that sort of thing here, because we have in the party across the way a curious heterogeneous mixture. In fact, when I was listening to the hon. member for Vancouver South I was reminded of the story of the chameleon that was placed on a piece of tartan, and that blew up and bust. Certainly the Liberal party today represents a strange hodge-podge. It has at least a checkerboard effect that may well result in that unhappy end for the hon. member for Vancouver South.
We have here a bill about which we know very little. All we have before us is an outline of a bill. We do not know the most important aspect of this legislation. We do not know what is going to be the interpretation of the term "totally disabled", because that will be decided by regulation. Presumably it will be decided by that great and good cabinet, possibly speaking through the mouth of an inspired Minister of National Health and Welfare.
We do not know yet who in Canada will be covered by this legislation. All we know is that whoever they are they will be covered inadequately, after a long period of waiting, in which organizations and people throughout Canada have been appealing in the past to this government to take some action.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not speak at length on this measure for the very good reason that I have already expressed my opinion on several occasions in the House of Commons as to the necessity for having pensions for -disabled persons. Secondly, I do not think at this stage of the session we should have long debates. I believe they should be avoided if possible.
However I cannot let this opportunity pass to hail this great forward step in our program of social security. I was listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) a little while ago when he said

that he sat on the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate which looked into this matter of social security in the year 1950. I sat with the hon. member on that committee, and at that time we worked in harmony. Therefore I am surprised by the lack of harmony in this debate.
I was sure our friends on the other side of the house, particularly hon. members in the C.C.F., would congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) upon the legislation he has introduced, and would support it unstintingly. But there is not even harmony among members of the C.C.F. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, "We welcome this legislation." That was the first speech for that party made in this debate. But the reaction of that party to this legislation has been deteriorating throughout the debate, to the point where we now hear the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) describing the legislation as very inadequate and very mediocre.
I suggest that those in the opposition who reproach members on this side of the house for injecting politics into the debate should look to their own side before throwing reproaches like that at this side. Because when I hear members in the opposition describing this legislation as very mediocre, then they are certainly playing politics in a very important matter, a matter which is very important to the people of Canada, and a matter with which no one should play politics.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he say that this legislation is adequate?

I would say that it is certainly adequate under the circumstances-and that is the next point I will come to. I agree with the opposition that it will be important to define clearly what is meant by total disability. I realize there will be certain difficulty raised for members of parliament who will have to cope with constituents who claim that they are totally disabled when, in fact, they may not be completely covered by the definition which will be given.
But I do say in all sincerity that under the circumstances, when we consider the very heavy burden our country has to carry in taxes for national defence, and when we consider the fact that we have had to support the Korean war, and that nearly half our budget is turned over for national defence, we must be convinced that this is adequate legislation, indeed. And we should be very proud of it. Sincere congratulations are due the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)

and the Minister of National Health and Welfare for having introduced this legislation.
